items.abstract_text: Abstract Children today grow up in a hybrid physical and digital environment, engaging with mobile devices from an early age, which poses a risk of negatively impacting their development. This usage often replaces social interactions and physical activities, potentially deteriorating relationships, socio-cognitive skills, and mental health. Banning device use is unrealistic, but the way children use mobiles can be altered through responsible technology. In the present study we (1) explored parental expectations regarding children’s mobile applications, (2) directlyincorporated these expectations into the design of a specific application (Alphie), and (3) examined its reception through UX testing. Alphie is a child-focused application (launcher) that promotes social interaction, real-world activities, and reduces solitary screen time. Its design is informed by parental expectations and scientific data, emphasizing educational, age-appropriate, and moderately stimulating content, with parental control features. A user study with parent-child dyads showed positive experiences. Notably, the games requiring active parental involvement were also well-received, suggesting that they are effective tools for facilitating joint activities within the family. This research highlights how responsible technology can support the mental and physical health of the new generation. By linking parental expectations, application design, and user experience within a single framework, the present studyprovides a more integrative perspective on the development and evaluation of child-focused digital applications.

items.abstract_text: Abstract The development and ubiquitous availability of large language model based systems (LLMs) poses a plurality of potentials and risks for education in schools and universities. In this paper, we provide an analysis and discussion of the overreliance concern as one specific risk: that students might fail to acquire important skills, or be inhibited in the acquisition of these skills, because they overly rely on LLMs. We use the distinction between local and global goals of education to guide our investigation. In our view, the harm of LLM overreliance is specifically that it severs the connection between local educational goals (e.g., successfully solving a specific kind of math problem) and global educational goals (e.g., acquiring general skills for mathematics). Based on this analysis, we sketch three possible responses to the overreliance concern: preserving both local and global goals while making minimal changes to educational practice (a conservative approach), changing global and local educational goals (a revisionary perspective), and preserving global educational goals while changing local goals (an in-between view). Since different types of responses have different benefits and weaknesses, we think that it is likely that an optimal response ultimately combines elements from all three types.

items.abstract_text: Despite growing interest in generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) in higher education, limited attention has been paid to how learning engagement is reconfigured in GenAI-assisted contexts and how it supports critical thinking. This study adopts a grounded theory approach to examine the dimensions of postgraduate learning engagement and its underlying mechanisms. Based on semi-structured interviews with 32 postgraduates, four dimensions are identified: cognitive, emotional, human-AI interaction, and agentic engagement. Extending existing frameworks, the findings show that engagement promotes critical thinking through both direct and indirect pathways. Learning self-efficacy and lower-order cognitive offloading act as key mediators, while GenAI trust serves as a contextual moderator. A process-oriented model is proposed to explain how GenAI reshapes engagement and fosters higher-order thinking.

items.abstract_text: Generative AI systems are increasingly used by older adults with cognitive impairment for everyday tasks such as information seeking, health management, and communication. While these systems provide flexible, language-based support, their open-ended outputs introduce risks of over-reliance, misinterpretation, and inappropriate decision-making. Prior work has focused on usability and adoption, with limited attention to how system design shapes users’ participation in decision-making and the distribution of agency in care contexts. We present a qualitative study of 45 individuals with cognitive impairment and their caregivers. We identify five accessibility-oriented mechanisms: AI Capability Constraint, Human Oversight Embedding, Cognitive Engagement Maintenance, Human–AI Relationship Regulation, and Risk Transparency and Control, through which systems structure interaction. These mechanisms both support and constrain users by redistributing decision-making across users and caregivers. We show that their effects vary by impairment level: while protective mechanisms support users with severe impairment, they can restrict autonomy for those with mild impairment. As impairment progresses, tensions become less visible as user participation diminishes. Our findings highlight the need for dynamic designs that balance safety and autonomy in AI-supported care.

items.title: What the submission does not show: Complexifying cognitive offloading in students' mathematical work with LLMs
items.abstract_text: A common concern is that using large language models (LLMs) lets students offload mathematical work that tasks are designed to elicit. Yet such claims often rest on outcomes (e.g., submitted solutions), rather than on evidence of students' work with LLMs. We followed 23 first-year linear algebra students as they solved three differently designed homework tasks with LLMs. Drawing on self-regulated learning and choice-affluent environments, we interpreted each of 429 prompts as a trace of a regulatory event and compared 59 chatlogs with the problem solutions the students submitted. Prompts formed five structures, casting the LLM mainly as a solver, explainer, or validator. The mix of structures shifted across the tasks, and ten of the 15 students who completed all three tasks changed their dominant structure. Most final submissions stayed close to LLM output, including those that followed exchanges in which students had explained, conjectured, and checked their own ideas. We conclude that an LLM-aided submission is not a trustworthy marker of students' offloading of the mathematical work, and that offloading needs to be examined in each regulatory space and part by part rather than as a whole.

items.abstract_text: Individuals with Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD) typically perform cognitive tasks with greater response time variability than matched peers. This is thought to be due to the greater occurrence of occasional extremely slow responses associated with lowered arousal levels. To test this we designed a new, less arousing task to measure sustained attention, named the Disappearance Detection Task (DDT). This study aimed to investigate the relationship between response time variability and levels of ADHD symptoms both in this new, low-arousal sustained attention task and in the Sustained Attention to Response Task (SART). Twenty-eight children and 49 adolescents participated. On both tasks, ADHD symptom levels were associated with response time variability measures of SDRT and tau, but not with sigma. On the DDT, children with higher ADHD symptoms made more commission errors and were less accurate in detecting the target (d'), whereas adolescents made a similar number of commission errors and d' irrespective of their ADHD symptom levels. This pattern was not present in the SART. The adolescents found the DDT more challenging than the SART as their target sensitivity was lower during the DDT. The children were less confident in nominating the target (criterion) during the DDT than the SART. The results indicate that RTV measures are more consistently associated with ADHD symptoms than other RT measures and that the DDT is a sensitive task of sustained attention and response inhibition performance, particularly in children, and in children with higher symptoms of ADHD.

items.abstract_text: Abstract Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) offers learners immediate and personalized support, yet unguided interaction may encourage passive use and weaken self-regulated learning (SRL). This study examined whether question-chain prompting can support SRL in human-AI interaction. A quasi-experiment was conducted with 83 undergraduates enrolled in a television program production course. A control group used free-form questioning, whereas two experimental groups used either a progressive or a divergent question-chain strategy. Data included GenAI interaction logs, post-task reflections, metacognitive awareness measures, and course grades. This study found that both question-chain groups demonstrated significantly more learning-strategy and learning-monitoring behaviors than the control group. Reflection data further indicated differences in students’ approaches to human-AI collaboration, although these differences should be interpreted cautiously because the reflection prompts differed by condition. Moreover, both experimental groups scored significantly higher than the control group on knowledge of cognition, regulation of cognition, and academic achievement. No significant differences were found between the progressive and divergent question-chain approaches. The findings suggest that question-chain prompting, implemented as an instructional package of specific, sequenced, and required questions, can promote more active engagement during human-AI interaction and support metacognitive development and learning performance. Question chains offer a practical approach for guiding students’ use of GenAI in educational settings.

reading.interpretation: This study examined whether question-chain strategies can be used to structure learners' interactions with GenAI and whether different forms of question chains produce different effects. Compared with free-form questioning, both progressive and divergent question-chain strategies were associated with more learning regulation behaviors, higher metacognitive awareness, and higher academic achievement. However, no significant differences were found between the two question-chain approaches. These findings should be interpreted as effects of the question-chain conditions as a whole. Compared with the control condition, the question chains differed simultaneously in the specificity and quality of the prescribed questions, their sequence, the requirement that each question build on the preceding response, the requirement to complete every step, and the wording of the reflection prompts. The present design therefore cannot attribute the observed differences to chaining per se, and the mechanisms discussed below should be read as possible explanations rather than demonstrated causal pathways. Regarding students' regulation of learning behaviors, analysis of the interaction logs showed that both experimental groups demonstrated more learning-strategy and learning-monitoring behaviors than the control group. The largest difference appeared in learning monitoring. This result is consistent with the possibility that the question-chain conditions changed how students engaged with AI responses. The three instruction sheets shared the same general sections, which specified the work requirements (a 5-10-minute short film on a self-selected theme), the submission requirements, and the availability of production equipment and teacher consultation. Students therefore decided which issues to ask about, how to formulate their questions, and how to continue or revise the dialogue based on the AI's responses. The conditions therefore differed mainly in the specificity of the prompts, their prescribed sequence, the requirement that each question build on the preceding response, and the requirement to complete every step. analysis.discussion: This study examined whether question-chain strategies can be used to structure learners' interactions with GenAI and whether different forms of question chains produce different effects. Compared with free-form questioning, both progressive and divergent question-chain strategies were associated with more learning regulation behaviors, higher metacognitive awareness, and higher academic achievement. However, no significant differences were found between the two question-chain approaches. These findings should be interpreted as effects of the question-chain conditions as a whole. Compared with the control condition, the question chains differed simultaneously in the specificity and quality of the prescribed questions, their sequence, the requirement that each question build on the preceding response, the requirement to complete every step, and the wording of the reflection prompts. The present design therefore cannot attribute the observed differences to chaining per se, and the mechanisms discussed below should be read as possible explanations rather than demonstrated causal pathways. Regarding students' regulation of learning behaviors, analysis of the interaction logs showed that both experimental groups demonstrated more learning-strategy and learning-monitoring behaviors than the control group. The largest difference appeared in learning monitoring. This result is consistent with the possibility that the question-chain conditions changed how students engaged with AI responses. Under the question-chain design, each new question had to build on the previous response. This requirement may have led students to read, evaluate, and connect AI-generated information before continuing the interaction. Such engagement, if it occurred, would be consistent with the constructive and interactive forms of engagement associated with stronger learning outcomes (Chi & Wylie, 2014) . The finding is consistent with previous research showing that guided questioning promotes knowledge construction and comprehension monitoring (King, 1994; Rosenshine et al., 1996) . However, some coded behaviors, such as knowledge expansion and content evaluation, were partly embedded in the prescribed questions themselves (e.g., the final review step of the progressive chain). The higher frequencies may therefore partly reflect compliance with the prescribed prompts, and the effect of question specificity cannot be separated from that of the chained structure. The reflection data offer tentative evidence of differences in how students engaged with GenAI. This evidence is weaker than that from the interaction logs because the reflection prompts differed by condition and explicitly cued some of the coded themes. Students in the experimental groups described more deliberate interaction strategies, including precise prompting, iterative refinement, and selective use of AI suggestions. Control-group reflections, meanwhile, concerned the information GenAI provided and its perceived limitations. Taken together, the interaction logs and reflection data suggest that question-chain prompting was associated with more active forms of engagement during human-AI dialogue. In terms of students' metacognitive awareness, both experimental groups scored significantly higher than the control group on knowledge of cognition and regulation of cognition. A possible explanation is that question chains supported metacognitive processes within the interaction itself. The questions may have encouraged students to evaluate responses against their goals and consider whether to accept, revise, or reject the content; however, this process was neither explicitly required nor established by the reported analyses. These activities correspond closely to the planning, monitoring, and evaluation processes that characterize metacognitive regulation (Bannert & Reimann, 2012; Schraw & Dennison, 1994) . The present findings are consistent with previous research showing that metacognitive scaffolds can promote deeper cognitive processing in GenAI-supported learning environments (Wu et al., 2025) . The findings also contribute to ongoing discussions regarding the potential metacognitive risks of GenAI. Fan et al. (2025) reported that unstructured ChatGPT use was associated with reductions in metacognitive processes, a pattern they described as metacognitive laziness. The current results suggest that these outcomes may depend partly on how learners interact with the technology. When questioning is structured and supported by specific, well-formulated prompts, students may engage more actively in monitoring and regulating their learning. From the perspective of Winne and Hadwin (1998) , question chains provide external support that may help learners initiate and sustain monitoring processes during AI-supported learning. Furthermore, this study found that students in both experimental groups achieved significantly higher grades than those in the control group. This result is consistent with extensive evidence linking self-regulated learning to academic performance (Zimmerman, 2002) . It also aligns with previous studies showing that GenAI is most effective when integrated into structured instructional activities (Deng et al., 2025; Li et al., 2025) . One possible explanation is that structured questioning encouraged students to engage more deeply with intermediate products throughout the project. Students may have examined and revised scripts and production plans during the interaction, although this process was not established by the reported analyses. This iterative process may have contributed to stronger final products and, consequently, higher grades. Alternatively, the specific and carefully formulated prompts may have elicited higher-quality AI output that directly improved the scripts, independent of any change in students' regulation. Although the question-chain groups outperformed the control group across all three outcomes, no significant differences emerged between the progressive and divergent approaches. This finding may indicate that the effectiveness of question chains depends more on the presence of structure than on the specific form of the chain. However, because both chains also shared prompt specificity and required completion, this comparison cannot isolate the contribution of chaining itself. Both approaches required students to build each question on the previous response and were intended to support active engagement with AI-generated information. This interpretation is consistent with scaffolding theory, which emphasizes structured guidance while preserving learner agency (Wood et al., 1976) . The absence of significant differences also suggests that instructors may be able to select either approach depending on instructional goals and task characteristics. The study has several theoretical and practical implications. Theoretically, it extends question-chain research from teacher-student interaction to human-AI interaction. It also points to structured questioning as a potential means through which self-regulated learning may be supported in GenAI-assisted environments, although the present design cannot determine which components of the question chains were responsible. In addition, the findings contribute to current discussions about cognitive offloading and passive AI use (Fan et al., 2025; Risko & Gilbert, 2016) . items.abstract_text: The rapid adoption of generative artificial intelligence (generative AI) in higher education has raised concerns about its impact on students' critical thinking in academic writing, yet evidence on the conditions under which the two are related remains inconsistent. This quantitative correlational study examined the relationship between generative AI use and critical thinking among 34 Indonesian Language and Literature Education (PBSI) students participating in the Merdeka Student Exchange Program (PMM) when writing scientific articles. Drawing on Social Cognitive Theory and the cognitive offloading perspective, generative AI use was measured through four indicators (frequency, purpose, dependence, and AI literacy), and critical thinking through five aspects (analysis, evaluation, inference, synthesis–explanation, and reflection), using a four-point Likert questionnaire. Data were analyzed using simple and multiple linear regression, an independent-samples t-test, and moderated hierarchical regression. Composite generative AI use was not linearly related to critical thinking (p = .131) but showed an inverted-U pattern (p = .010), and intensive and selective users did not differ significantly (p = .097). AI literacy moderated the relationship between usage intensity and critical thinking (?R² = .222, p = .004; Holm-adjusted p = .016), with a significant positive relationship only among students with above-average AI literacy. These findings indicate that strengthening AI literacy in academic writing instruction, rather than merely restricting generative AI use, should underpin responsible, literacy-based generative AI policies in higher education.

This finding underscores that what matters is not how much students use generative AI but whether such use is accompanied by the ability to evaluate and control AI output. The high mean levels of generative AI use and critical thinking should be interpreted in light of the respondents' characteristics. All respondents had completed a scientific article writing course, and two-thirds of them combined more than one AI tool, particularly ChatGPT, Gemini, and Quillbot. This pattern is consistent with Febriani et al. (2023) , who showed that students used Quillbot and ChatGPT mainly for paraphrasing and grammar correction, and with Chan and Hu (2023) , who found that students perceived generative AI as a useful aid that also raised academic concerns. The invalidity of four of the six usage purpose items is also substantively meaningful: items asking about the use of AI to generate ideas, outline articles, edit language, and understand concepts were answered relatively uniformly, suggesting that these purposes have become common practices that no longer differentiate students. What differentiated respondents were the items concerning the replacement of ideas, such as asking AI to write entire sections of an article or using AI to avoid generating one's own ideas. The nonsignificant Ha1 result differs from the finding of Hutauruk et al. (2025) , who reported a low but positive correlation (r = .377) between generative chatbot use and critical thinking in academic writing, and it also does not replicate the negative associations reported by Zou et al. (2023) and Gerlich (2025) . Two factors may explain this difference. First, the linearity test showed that the relationship between the composite X score and critical thinking was quadratic, with the middle-tertile group obtaining the highest critical thinking scores; this nonlinear pattern may mask the actual relationship when tested with a linear model. Second, the composite score combines dimensions that operate in different directions: more measured usage frequency tended to be accompanied by higher critical thinking (albeit nonsignificantly), whereas lower dependence was accompanied by lower critical thinking, so that the two tendencies cancel each other out at the composite level. This explanation aligns with Chan's (2023) view that generative AI use is multidimensional and cannot be reduced to a single measure. The Ha2 result also differs from Santoso and Patrissia (2026) , who found differences in critical thinking across usage-intensity groups. Although the effect size was medium (d = 0.71), the difference in this study was not significant, likely because each group contained only 12 respondents, limiting statistical power. From the perspective of Social Cognitive Theory, usage intensity alone is insufficient to explain critical thinking when cognitive factors such as AI literacy and self-regulation are not taken into account. The finding that deserves the closest attention is the partial relationship of dependence intensity (X3): respondents who reported greater dependence on generative AI rated their critical thinking higher. This finding contrasts with Zhai et al. (2024) and Gerlich (2025) , who showed that overreliance risks diminishing cognitive abilities through cognitive offloading. The discrepancy is most likely related to how variable Y was measured. Because critical thinking in this study was self-reported, students who frequently rely on generative AI may judge their thinking ability based on the quality of AI-assisted manuscripts rather than on the thinking processes they actually perform a phenomenon consistent with the concept of metacognitive laziness (Fan et al., 2025) . Faqih and Ridwan (2026) likewise found that AI improved the linguistic quality of writing without strengthening analytical or reflective thinking. Thus, the X3 finding is better interpreted as an indication of a gap between perceived and actual critical thinking ability, which should be verified through manuscript-based rubric assessment. The correlations in Table 6 suggest that the X3 finding is not confined to a single aspect, although none survived FDR correction, as the negative relationship appeared consistently across all five critical thinking aspects, with the strongest correlations for evaluation, inference, and reflection. These three aspects are precisely those that depend most on self-assessment: students must judge whether their sources are credible, whether their conclusions are supported by data, and whether their ideas genuinely originate from their own thinking. (2024) reported that generative AI is helpful in the early stages of writing but may limit students' independent analysis and evaluation; if this limitation goes unrecognized, AI-dependent students may overestimate their evaluative and reflective abilities. Hamsiah et al. items.abstract_text:
Abstract 
                   Objective: Deficits in attention have been linked to poorer performance on executive functioning tasks, particularly those requiring inhibition and cognitive flexibility. While continuous performance tests are commonly used to assess sustained attention, their relationship to error based executive outcomes under increased task demand in pediatric clinical populations remains incompletely characterized. This study examined whether performance on a relatively low demand task of sustained attention, the Conners’ Continuous Performance Test–Third Edition (CPT-3), predicts performance on a higher demand executive task, the Delis–Kaplan Executive Function System (D-KEFS) Color Word Interference Test (CW). Method/Data Selection: Data were obtained from a mixed clinical sample of 213 children and adolescents ages 8–17 years (M = 11.7, SD = 2.8; 47.8% male, 52.2% female) evaluated in an outpatient private practice neuropsychology clinic. Participants completed the CPT-3 and D-KEFS CW as part of individualized comprehensive neuropsychological batteries. Multivariate regression analyses examined whether CPT-3 subscales predicted performance on D-KEFS CW conditions. Results/Data Synthesis: The overall model significantly predicted D-KEFS Inhibition Error scores (R2 = .12, adjusted R2 = .08, F(9, 198) = 3.02, p = .002) and D-KEFS Inhibition/Switching Error scores (R2 = .17, adjusted R2 = .13, F(9, 198) = 4.56, p &lt; .001). CPT-3 reaction time–based indices accounted for the majority of explained variance across both error outcomes. Conclusions: Performance on a sustained attention task was associated with error based executive performance requiring inhibition and cognitive flexibility in this pediatric clinical sample. Faster response speed and higher variability in response speed may be linked more impulsive verbal responding, resulting in higher errors on a cognitively demanding task.

items.abstract_text: Generative AI tools and conversational chatbots are increasingly embedded in education, work, and daily life, raising concerns about engagement that becomes difficult to self-regulate. This review synthesizes emerging research on problematic generative AI use, treating addiction-like language as part of a broader problematic-use construct rather than a clinical diagnosis. Following PRISMA 2020 reporting, a Scopus search executed identified 188 records. Included studies were characterised by research design and evidence type rather than scored with a formal risk-of-bias instrument. Measurement work is expanding quickly, but instruments remain partially fragmented, blurring the boundary between high engagement, habitual reliance, and impairment. Mechanism studies converge on attachment processes, anthropomorphism and perceived empathy, loneliness and social anxiety, immersive flow, and self-regulatory strain, suggesting that social presence and immersion amplify reliance for some users. In learning and knowledge work, performance pressure and incentive structures can normalize overreliance, with reported risks for cognitive offloading, independent thinking, academic integrity, and skill development. Outcome studies associate compulsive or dependent use with technostress, psychological distress, and lower wellbeing, while mitigation discussion highlights reinforcement-friendly interface cues, privacy and memory governance, and sustainability trade-offs. Because the corpus is almost entirely cross-sectional and self-reported, these relationships are associations rather than causal effects. The key distinction is not between users and non-users, but between bounded, purpose-driven use and escalating reliance with reduced self-regulation. An Antecedents–Decisions–Outcomes structure is used only to frame a forward-looking agenda for longitudinal and intervention research. A sensitivity analysis comparing studies published in 2026 with those published earlier showed that no conclusion was reversed: the design profile and principal gaps held, while the most recent longitudinal studies strengthened the evidence on temporal order and outcomes.

items.abstract_text: Purpose This study aims to examine how customers perceive and engage with generative artificial intelligence (GenAI)-enabled services provided by small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs), with a particular focus on value co-creation and well-being outcomes. While prior studies have mainly investigated GenAI adoption from the firm perspective, this research shifts attention to customer-level psychological and experiential mechanisms in an emerging economy context. Design/methodology/approach Drawing on service-dominant logic and Sustainable Development Goal 3, the study adopts a quantitative approach. Data were collected from 180 Vietnamese consumers, predominantly educated youths aged 18–24, who had prior experience with GenAI-powered services offered by SMEs. Partial least squares structural equation modeling was used to test the proposed hypotheses. Findings The results indicate that perceived knowledge about GenAI and perceived marketplace influence are positively associated with customers’ value co-creation behavior. Value co-creation is positively associated with both value-in-use and emotional well-being. In addition, value-in-use is positively associated with perceptions of social well-being, whereas emotional well-being is not significantly associated with social well-being. Originality/value This study extends GenAI research by moving beyond firm-level adoption to examine customer-centric outcomes in SME service contexts in an emerging economy. It highlights perceived knowledge and marketplace influence as critical antecedents of value co-creation and demonstrates how AI-enabled services contribute to social value primarily through functional value-in-use rather than emotional pathways.

In line with previous literature emphasizing the experiential nature of value (Grönroos and Voima, 2013), H3 confirms that value co-creation is positively associated with value-in-use. This result strengthens the understanding that collaborative interactions between customers and GenAI-enabled SMEs lead to enhanced personalized service outcomes. Furthermore, H4 highlights the emotional benefits of co-creation, aligning with affective events theory (Weiss and Cropanzano, 1996) and extending the findings of Kim (2023), who observed emotional satisfaction in service innovation contexts, but without the GenAI lens. The Downloaded from www.​emerald.​com/​jsibr/​article-pdf/​2/​3/​128/​11866458/​jsibr-04-2025-0042en.​pdf by guest on 24 September 2026 relationship between value-in-use and social well-being offers a novel contribution by linking microlevel service outcomes with macrolevel societal perceptions, a connection that remains underexplored in GenAI literature (Creely and Blannin, 2025; Emerald Publishing, 2025). Finally, the results for H6 indicate that emotional well-being is not positively associated with perceptions of social well-being, providing an interesting insight to the broader validation of SDG 3 (Good Health and Well-being) in AI-powered service contexts. While emotional well- being contributes to individual satisfaction and psychological fulfillment, its effect may not extend to how customers evaluate collective or societal well-being. This outcome could stem from measurement boundaries that capture primarily individual affective states rather than socially oriented outcomes, or from cultural tendencies that distinguish personal emotions from community-based judgments. It may also reflect a theoretical misalignment, as affective responses often occur at an individual level, whereas social well-being reflects evaluative, relational and ethical considerations. These findings suggest that SMEs should make their societal and community contributions more visible and explicitly connect personalized GenAI services with inclusive, transparent and socially responsible practices. This study makes several important contributions to the literature on GenAI, value co- creation and social impact within the context of SMEs. First, this study advances the social impact literature by providing empirical evidence on how customers experience and derive value from GenAI-enabled services. It establishes that social impact in AI-mediated SME contexts is not solely a technological outcome, but a human-centered process shaped by customer perceptions, engagement and co-creation behaviors (Baabdullah, 2024; Dwivedi et al., 2023). The findings show that GenAI can serve as a social enabler when customers perceive transparency, control and personalization, reinforcing the idea that responsible AI deployment in SMEs can enhance community trust and shared well-being. Second, by integrating perceived knowledge and perceived marketplace influence as antecedents of value co-creation, this study enriches SDL theory (Vargo and Lusch, 2004, 2008) with a dual-path cognitive–normative model that explains why customers engage with Downloaded from www.​emerald.​com/​jsibr/​article-pdf/​2/​3/​128/​11866458/​jsibr-04-2025-0042en.​pdf by guest on 24 September 2026 GenAI-driven services. The results reveal that customers’ sense of agency and understanding Journal of Social of AI functions jointly motivate participation in value creation, underscoring that value-in- Impact in use emerges through meaningful human and AI collaboration rather than technological Business automation alone (Simón et al., 2024). Third, the nonsignificant relationship between Research emotional well-being and social well-being offers a nuanced theoretical contribution. It suggests that while GenAI interactions may enhance individual emotional satisfaction (e.g. personalization and convenience), they do not automatically translate into perceived social 141 connectedness or collective benefit. This finding highlights a “human disconnect” in GenAI- mediated service encounters, where emotional gratification remains individual rather than communal, signaling a need for SMEs to design AI experiences that visibly foster inclusion, empathy and societal contribution (Lin Li et al., 2025; Modgil et al., 2025). Finally, drawing on the Yi and Gong (2013) co-creation framework, this study identifies that behaviors such as providing feedback, adapting preferences and cooperating with AI interfaces contribute more strongly to social well-being perceptions than mere information sharing. items.title: Cognitive Task Substitution, Cognitive Offloading, and Behavioral Dependency on Artificial Intelligence-Assisted Technologies: A Scoping Review
items.preview: The rapid proliferation of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) and automated decision systems has resulted in a fundamental shift in human-technology interaction. items.abstract_text: The rapid proliferation of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) and automated decision systems has resulted in a fundamental shift in human-technology interaction. This scoping review aims to map the breadth of empirical evidence and original conceptual models regarding human-artificial intelligence (AI) functional displacement. The objective is to synthesize findings across disparate fields into a unified framework of task substitution, cognitive offloading, and behavioral dependency. This review followed the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses extension for Scoping Reviews (PRISMA-ScR) guidelines. Systematic searches were executed across PubMed, Scopus, the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials, and ScienceDirect. The studies were screened for research addressing thinking substitution (e.g., reasoning, clinical diagnosis, and creative synthesis) over simple digital assistance. A total of 36 studies met the inclusion criteria. Neurophysiological data from functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) indicate that digital saving triggers cognitive offloading, characterized by significantly lower activation in the right dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (DLPFC). In academic settings, randomized controlled trial data showed that students using ChatGPT scored significantly lower on 45-day retention tests (57.5% correct) compared to traditional learners (68.5% correct, p = 0.002). Professional judgment is increasingly subject to biases; MRI interpretation exhibited substantial self-anchoring bias (score: 6.94), while the automation bias index was high for ECG tasks (0.30). Senior executives receiving AI recommendations acted more actively (M = 5.05) than human-led controls (M = 4.61; p = 0.020), and 89% of educators surveyed reported perceptions of quantifiable skill atrophy. Socially, AI usage and human interaction were moderately and negatively correlated (r = -0.443; p < 0.01), with participants delaying the revelation of intentions in parallel-play settings with digital agents. Task substitution may create a "sovereignty trap" where individuals cede intellectual judgment to automated systems, confusing operational fluency with epistemic mastery. This reliance carries the risk of bypassing the desirable difficulties essential for long-term knowledge retention and the development of professional expertise. As "quiet dependency" becomes an evolving reality of professional and academic life, institutional and design-level interventions must prioritize trust-enabling mechanisms and robust AI literacy to preserve human critical character and professional autonomy.

items.preview: Cancellation tasks are widely used measures of attention but are conventionally scored by metrics such as mean accuracy or concentration scores, disregarding the temporal structure of responding. items.abstract_text: Cancellation tasks are widely used measures of attention but are conventionally scored by metrics such as mean accuracy or concentration scores, disregarding the temporal structure of responding. Here, we derive two reaction-time (RT) biomarkers from our tablet-based UCancellation task in 388 young adults: intra-individual RT variability (RTV), a marker of sustained attention, and switch cost, an index of cognitive flexibility from transitions between two different task's target categories. Because consecutive targets are separated by a variable number of scanned distractors, both are confounded by search effort, which we remove with a scanning-load (p) correction framework. RTV behaved as a scored individual-difference measure: correction improved reliability and convergent validity against TOVA low-frequency RTV (n = 373), and a cross-target composite was the most reliable index. Switch cost behaved as a within-task phenomenon whose sign reversed with load—large and positive when targets were adjacent, reversing as scanning load increased—consistent with inhibition of return. Together, these metrics show that RT structure within a brief cancellation task carries attentional information that standard metrics alone does not capture.

items.title: Too Long to Watch, Too Short to Leave: Designing for Agent Micro-Waits
items.abstract_text: Agentic systems increasingly carry out complex work, where a single turn routinely runs for minutes. This produces a micro-wait that is too long to watch and too short to leave. In a formative study with 12 daily agent users, we found that staying felt like wasted time, while switching away fragmented attention and forfeited the context needed to re-engage. We introduce Sidecar, a parallel assistant situated in the same interface as the agent, which reads the run and surfaces implicit decisions the agent made, along with task directions worth exploring. In a within-subjects study (N=16), Sidecar helped participants stay focused on their main task, freely workshop unfinished ideas without fear of unwanted action, and recognize under-specification in their own prompts. Together, these findings contribute to designs that help users stay context-aware and engaged during agent micro-waits.

items.abstract_text: Children born today enter a world in which artificial intelligence systems collect, categorize, and predict from the moment of birth, often before any digital engagement and well before the capacity to consent. Existing legal frameworks address children primarily as platform users defined by an age threshold or as natural persons without operational protection during incapacity, and none adequately addresses the newborn as a rights-bearing subject of algorithmic systems from the moment of birth. This paper proposes sovereignty-in-trust as the doctrinal frame within which children’s rights attach at birth and are held in trust during the period before consent capacity, with cognitive autonomy as the substantive content of what is held. The framework is derived from a literature review of the established provisions of the UN Convention on the Rights of the Child, read with the Committee’s General Comments, supported by data-protection and AI-governance instruments in the European Union, and refined through the supported-decision-making framework of the Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities. The paper highlights four key failure modes in current frameworks: regulatory overload, commercial monetization, dependence on political will, and the limitations of current doctrinal structures. It outlines five legal measures to enhance resilience: mandatory disclosure during neonatal data collection, a bankruptcy-proof restriction on transferring data from minors, automatic deletion or anonymization of identity data not explicitly retained, a safeguard against predictive profiling without prior consent, and ongoing ethical reform and liability across the AI product lifecycle. The paper advocates that the United Nations Committee on the Rights of the Child issue a new General Comment specifically addressing children’s rights in algorithmic systems, with dedicated provisions for the period before children have the capacity to give consent. The doctrinal objective is not to establish a new right but to articulate the operational form of existing rights as they apply to a subject who is currently unable to exercise them at the moment they attach.

items.abstract_text: Abstract While generative AI (GenAI) tools are emerging as educational resources, general‐purpose applications like ChatGPT are not explicitly designed to support the metacognitive and socio‐emotional dimensions of learning, often failing to address students' emotional states or promote independent thinking. In response, this study introduces a CVT‐SRL GenAI Support Framework integrating control‐value theory (CVT) and self‐regulated learning (SRL) and tests a learner‐centred GenAI chatbot design employing prompt‐based SRL scaffolding and emotional support. In a preregistered experiment in an authentic educational setting, 144 high school students were randomly assigned to one of three conditions: (1) ChatGPT, (2) SRLbot (GenAI with SRL scaffolding), (3) emotional SRLbot (GenAI with SRL and emotional support). Outcomes included conceptual knowledge and transfer, trace‐based and self‐reported engagement in SRL phases (forethought, performance, self‐reflection), enjoyment, boredom, hopelessness, self‐efficacy and trust. Data were collected at pretest, posttest and 4‐week follow‐up. Across conditions, students showed improvements in conceptual knowledge and transfer from pretest to posttest, with no significant condition differences in post‐to‐follow‐up change. Both SRLbot and Emotional SRLbot were associated with higher self‐reported enjoyment and lower boredom than ChatGPT and elicited trace‐based SRL behaviours. reading.methods: A preregistered randomized classroom experiment assigned 144 Danish high-school students to standard ChatGPT, an AI chatbot that guided self-regulated learning (SRLbot), or the same approach with emotional support (Emotional SRLbot), with 48 participants in each condition. One learning session lasted about 25 minutes. Tests and surveys were administered before and after, and 85 students completed a four-week follow-up. Interaction traces were coded to examine self-regulatory behaviors.
reading.findings: All three groups improved on immediate conceptual-knowledge and learning-transfer tests; however, condition-by-time comparisons were not statistically significant for either outcome (p = .980 and p = .953). At the four-week follow-up, knowledge and transfer change likewise did not differ significantly between groups. Both SRL-based chatbot groups showed larger improvements in enjoyment and reductions in boredom than the general-purpose ChatGPT group. Emotional SRLbot also showed higher task-level performance and reflection indicators in the interaction traces. Hopelessness fell across all groups without a differential treatment effect, and self-efficacy and chatbot trust did not show clear between-group benefits.
reading.interpretation: The authors interpret the findings as preliminary support for combining AI prompts about planning, monitoring and reflection with encouragement sensitive to students' emotional states. An intervention that makes learning feel better and increases momentary self-regulatory behavior is not yet evidence of lasting independent learning gains. Theoretical expectations about emotional regulation pathways were not themselves fully tested as causal mediators.
reading.limitations: The intervention lasted only one 25-minute session. The pretest and follow-up knowledge measures had internal consistency below .60, making the learning estimates less reliable. Only 85 of the original 144 returned for follow-up, and dropout related to prior AI experience and initial boredom. Some self-report and trace-based measures diverged, and trace coding was aggregated across each session rather than modeling the sequence of regulatory behaviors. Several outcome comparisons were tested and longer-term effects remain uncertain.

items.title: Why calling for a ‘kill switch’ is the wrong way to think about reining in AI
authors: Trent Wintermeier, Ph.D. Candidate in Rhetoric and Writing, The University of Texas at Austin
items.preview: A kill switch to shut down dangerous AI systems is a seductive concept, but the metaphor hides how the models work – and how they get out of control in the first place.

reading.overview: A kill switch to shut down dangerous AI systems is a seductive concept, but the metaphor hides how the models work – and how they get out of control in the first place.
reading.notice: This is a short description supplied by the publisher feed, not a full-article review or independent assessment.

source_review.thesis: The idea of a single emergency switch makes AI governance look like a matter of one decisive act. Wintermeier argues that this image hides the distributed infrastructure of advanced systems and the human decisions that shape their behavior before any emergency occurs.
source_review.reasoning: The essay treats a kill switch as a political and technological metaphor rather than only a device specification. A switch implies a bounded machine, an identifiable point of control and an operator who can intervene once a problem is visible. That mental picture is a poor fit for advanced AI deployed across interconnected services, data centers, models and users. Even if a particular model can be disabled, the metaphor does not specify who could halt associated processes or what would remain active elsewhere. Wintermeier connects this limitation to the familiar image of AI as a black box. Both metaphors encourage readers to imagine a single opaque object, instead of asking how infrastructures, organizations and choices interact. Crucially, the metaphor also places people outside the system until an emergency, concealing how training settings, permissions, supervision and deployment decisions were made throughout its operation.
source_review.examples: The author places 2026 proposals for an AI Kill Switch Act and state-level emergency safeguards in the context of politicians' analogies to mechanical emergency buttons. He also analyzes accounts of an AI-agent security incident involving Hugging Face. Some stories cast the agent as having acted on an independent agenda; Wintermeier points to the role of human choices around safety configurations, task expectations and internet access. The example illustrates why simply describing the model as rogue can distract from the organizational decisions that made its behavior possible. These examples explain the rhetorical frame; they should not be confused with experiments demonstrating that a particular intervention works or fails.
source_review.tension: Emergency interruption can still be one useful safeguard. The essay's criticism is directed at presenting a single switch as an adequate account of control, not at proving that all forms of technical shutdown are pointless. A practical governance strategy needs both enforceable interruption capabilities and a much wider account of authority, auditability, system dependencies and oversight before deployment. The original commentary does not offer an evaluated alternative regulatory framework or evidence about the effectiveness of particular policy designs.
source_review.implications: For agents that organize attention or act on a user's behalf, a clear stop or revoke button is necessary but not sufficient. Designers should also disclose whose instructions an agent follows, what permissions it holds, how people can review earlier actions, and which dependencies may keep working after an interaction is stopped. These are applications of Wintermeier's reasoning to attention technologies, not outcomes demonstrated by this article.
source_review.open_question: What would count as meaningful human control over an AI assistant if users cannot inspect the permissions, dependencies and decisions that shape its actions?
source_review.qualification: This is a rhetoric- and governance-centered expert commentary, not an empirical evaluation of frontier AI controls. It describes particular incidents and policy proposals from 2026; those circumstances are context for the author's argument, not a systematic sample of AI failures.

items.preview: AI coding interfaces present generated code either all at once or token-by-token. We argue that code rendering is a first-class interaction primitive that shapes how programmers read and understand code. To explore this design space, we introduce structured render…
items.abstract_text: AI coding interfaces present generated code either all at once or token-by-token. These rendering strategies reflect model generation rather than how programmers actually read code: selectively, non-linearly, and guided by the structure. We argue that code rendering is a first-class interaction primitive that shapes how programmers read and understand code. To explore this design space, we introduce structured rendering, a technique that reveals code in semantically meaningful chunks derived from its syntactic hierarchy, exposing high-level structure before low-level details. To isolate rendering effects on visual attention, we conducted an eye-tracking study with 53 participants comparing static, character-based, and structured rendering. Our findings show that rendering alters visual attention and reading behavior: dynamic rendering induces fewer but longer fixations and more sustained focus, while structured rendering further guides attention toward semantically meaningful units and supports high-level understanding. We release the anonymized dataset with an interactive demo (https://codegaze.vercel.app/) to support future research.

items.abstract_text: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is transforming the possibilities for informal language learning by providing immediate feedback, conversational interaction, and potentially personalized learning experiences. However, its use does not necessarily entail greater learner autonomy, self-regulation, or agency. This study aimed to understand how Colombian adults configure their informal English learning practices through GenAI tools, with particular attention to decision-making processes, self-regulation, evaluation of AI-generated responses, and the articulation of GenAI with other learning resources. Adopting a qualitative, exploratory, and interpretive approach, the study involved four Colombian adults with diverse linguistic, educational, and GenAI-use trajectories. Data were generated through participant characterization forms, GenAI interaction records, semi-structured interviews, and, when available, documentary evidence of participants’ interactions with the technology. A predominantly inductive thematic analysis generated four interconnected categories: negotiating control over the learning interaction; constructing and calibrating trust in AI-generated feedback; experiencing personalization through responsive interaction; and reconfiguring the broader learning repertoire. Findings show that participants assumed, negotiated, and delegated control in different ways and developed varying criteria for accepting, questioning, or verifying GenAI-generated responses. They also selectively integrated GenAI with other digital and human learning resources. Based on these findings, the study conceptualizes GenAI appropriation as a form of situated orchestration through which learners coordinate technological affordances with their purposes, prior knowledge, evaluative criteria, and broader learning repertoires. The findings suggest that GenAI does not automatically produce learner autonomy or agency; rather, it creates new spaces in which these may be exercised, negotiated, or delegated.

items.preview: This integrative literature review examines how generative artificial intelligence is shaping human thinking, cognitive processes and writing practices, with a focus on education across schools, universities, adult learning and professional settings. It considers how AI-supported composing alters the ways writers plan, generate, organise, revise and evaluate text, and how these changes reshape cognition, agency, aut…
items.abstract_text: This integrative literature review examines how generative artificial intelligence is shaping human thinking, cognitive processes and writing practices, with a focus on education across schools, universities, adult learning and professional settings. It considers how AI-supported composing alters the ways writers plan, generate, organise, revise and evaluate text, and how these changes reshape cognition, agency, authorship and learning. Rather than treating generative AI simply as a tool for productivity, the review approaches it as a relational technology that mediates meaning-making and textual production, while reserving the language of intentional agency for human actors. Thirty-six publications, identified through a structured search of seven information sources reported in accordance with PRISMA 2020 and appraised using criteria matched to each form of evidence, were synthesised thematically. Albert Bandura’s social cognitive theory provides the analytical lens, particularly triadic reciprocal causation, self-efficacy, observational learning, self-regulation and human agency. The discussion develops a critical account that recognises clear benefits while flagging risks of cognitive offloading, uncritical trust, homogenised expression and weakened metacognitive control. Claims are calibrated to the type of evidence supporting them, and findings drawn from preprints, small samples and self-report designs are presented as preliminary. The review advances a hybrid account in which human and machine contributions to composing are entwined and argues that this entwinement makes deliberate human participation more rather than less necessary. It concludes by proposing guidelines for educators across sectors, together with the assessment conditions under which those guidelines can be verified.

items.abstract_text: Effective collaboration and communication are vital to developer productivity and well-being, yet remain constrained by human factors such as attention, intrinsic motivation, and interpersonal accountability. These constraints are particularly vital for developers identifying with Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD), who navigate persistent environmental barriers in modern hybrid workplace settings. While developers with ADHD frequently rely on collaborative copresence practices (such as body doubling or pair programming) to support executive function, the recent emergence of agentic AI coding assistants has begun reshaping these collaborative dynamics. To investigate how developers with ADHD engage in human and AI-based copresence practices, we conducted semi-structured interviews with 14 software engineers with ADHD. Our findings reveal that while traditional human-human copresence provides critical social support and onboarding structure, it forces developers to constantly manage professional reputation and sacrifice personal privacy. Conversely, developers leverage emerging human-AI copresence to maintain accountability and cognitive flow without the social anxiety, performance judgment, or surveillance associated with human observation. Based on these empirical insights, we map developer copresence practices onto core dimensions of Goffman's copresence theory and Forsgren et al.'s SPACE framework of developer productivity, and provide design recommendations for AI-based tools that promote inclusive collaboration for developers with ADHD.

items.abstract_text: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is increasingly embedded in students’ learning and knowledge-work routines, yet perceived productivity gains do not necessarily arise from technology acceptance alone. This study develops and empirically examines an integrated Technology Acceptance Model (TAM) and Self-Regulated Learning (SRL) framework for explaining learning productivity among Google/Gemini users in Bangladesh. The study dataset contains 400 respondent IDs, of which 385 records contain complete questionnaire responses and a valid attention-check response; 15 rows are blank. The analysis therefore uses 385 usable cases and conducts an additional sensitivity analysis on 302 respondents classified as regular or occasional AI-feature users. Perceived ease of use (PEOU), perceived usefulness (PU), SRL and learning productivity (LP) were operationalised using three five-point Likert items each. Transparent composite-score path analysis with 5,000 bootstrap resamples was used because the available analytical environment did not contain a dedicated CFA/PLS-SEM implementation; consequently, the reported measurement diagnostics are explicitly treated as pre-publication validation evidence rather than as a claim of completed covariance-based CFA or PLS-SEM. PEOU positively predicted PU (β = .278, p &lt; .001), while both PEOU (β = .191, p &lt; .001) and PU (β = .218, p &lt; .001) predicted SRL. Learning productivity was predicted by PEOU (β = .140, p = .004), PU (β = .256, p &lt; .001) and SRL (β = .202, p &lt; .001), with R² = .188. Bootstrap estimates also supported indirect pathways from PEOU to LP through PU and SRL, including a serial PEOU → PU → SRL → LP effect. The results suggest that the productivity value of GenAI is partly behavioural: users benefit not only because the technology is perceived as useful and easy to operate, but also because those perceptions are associated with planning, monitoring and addressing learning gaps. The study contributes an emerging-market, mechanism-oriented account of GenAI-enabled learning productivity and identifies measurement and sampling issues that should be resolved in subsequent validation research.

items.abstract_text: The diffusion of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) across the creative industries has sharpened debates about automation, productivity, authorship, and the future of work. Attention has so far gravitated towards two poles: macro-level questions about job displacement, and technical questions about model performance and output quality. Much less has been said about how these systems are folded into the daily routines of professional work, and how that folding reorganises the conditions under which creative labour is performed, judged, and legitimated. This paper examines the incorporation of generative AI into advertising agencies, treated as strategic observatories of wider transformations in cognitive and creative labour. Drawing on a multi-method qualitative design that combines a scoping review with thirty-three in-depth semi-structured interviews with creative professionals, it traces how AI-assisted workflows are reorganised around selective delegation, cognitive offloading, iterative evaluation, orchestration, and what it terms curatorial labour: the emergent expertise of directing, evaluating, and taking responsibility for what algorithmic systems generate. Drawing on socio-technical accounts of distributed creativity, the paper argues that generative AI redistributes rather than replaces creative production, dispersing expertise, evaluative authority, and aesthetic judgment across human actors, machines, datasets, and commissioning organisations. It further argues that AI governance remains too model-centred and proposes a workflow-centred perspective on generative AI at work.

items.abstract_text: Drawing on a computational thinking model and cognitive offloading theory, this exploratory mixed-methods study examined whether structured AI scaffolding is associated with differential computational thinking (CT) outcomes and explored the role of metacognitive self-regulation. Two naturally occurring sections (n = 47) of the same liberal arts course, taught by the same instructor in consecutive Fall semesters, one embedding ChatGPT and one not, were compared using independent-samples t-tests, multiple regression, and inductive content analysis. Students in the ChatGPT-embedded section reported significantly higher problem-solving scores on a validated CT instrument. Digital literacy scores did not differ, possibly reflecting measurement limitations or the intervention's focus on reasoning over general digital fluency. Problem solving correlated significantly with metacognitive strategy use and contributed to a significant overall regression model, but did not remain a unique predictor after adjusting for digital literacy and class membership. Qualitative analysis identified three themes: ChatGPT as a cognitive scaffold, ChatGPT as a cognitive risk, and student-initiated boundary-setting. Most students expressed all three simultaneously, suggesting structured AI-embedded environments may foster metacognitive vigilance alongside CT gains. Findings support deliberate instructional design and explicit metacognitive supports when integrating ChatGPT in higher education.

items.preview: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is rapidly entering education, framed as a tool for efficiency and personalization. items.abstract_text: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is rapidly entering education, framed as a tool for efficiency and personalization. In this Perspective, we argue this obscures a deeper transformation. Schools are cognitive ecologies in which tools and social practices actively shape learning. GenAI restructures this ecology, redistributing epistemic labour, consolidating pedagogical functions, and reorganizing how knowledge is accessed, produced, and evaluated. Unlike most educational technologies, it is active, persistent, and generalist. We identify two enduring misalignments: a pedagogical gap between learning sciences and AI design, and a goal gap between measurable performance and developmental aims. Both gaps reflect logics already embedded within existing educational systems organized around efficiency, standardization, and control. GenAI does not introduce but risks entrenching and amplifying these gaps. Rather than accommodating GenAI through technical adjustments, we propose treating it as a diagnostic opportunity to redesign schooling for embodied, collaborative, and distinctly human forms of learning.

analysis.discussion: These considerations cannot be addressed by optimising individual tools or incrementally adjusting curricula. They require a broader reconfiguration. GenAI, precisely because it unsettles established assumptions about knowledge, authority, and learning, represents a catalytic opportunity to undertake it (for a summary, see Fig. 1 ). Fig. 1 Current Educational Logic vs Multitechnological Cognitive Ecology. This opportunity has precedent. The COVID-19 pandemic exposed the fragility of inherited educational arrangements with unprecedented clarity 31 , 33 . Yet, the prevailing response was restorative rather than transformative, focused on recovering what had been lost rather than reconsidering what might be built in its place 171 . Crises alone do not produce transformations, which require a prepared conceptual and practical vocabulary. The vocabulary for such a reconfiguration already exists. From Dewey’s learning by doing 172 to Papert’s constructionist vision of coding as epistemic practice 173 , from place-based education 174 to ‘Learning by Design’ 175 , 176 , from Bers’ framing of coding as a playground for young learners 177 to contemporary research on embodied learning environments 178 , and more powerfully, to Montessori’s prepared environment (e.g., refs. 93 , 179 – 182 , a rich lineage of educational theory and practice has long insisted that learning is most powerful when it is embodied, situated, collaborative, and materially grounded. What has been lacking is not the vision, but the institutional will, the technological ecology, and the socio-economic resources adequate to realise it. Realising it requires conceiving of education as a multi-technological cognitive ecology : a deliberately designed configuration of diverse material, social, and digital resources that jointly scaffold learning in ways consistent with what cognitive science tells us about human understanding 99 . Within such an ecology, no single technology dominates: low-tech, embodied, and collaborative tools are combined with digital and AI-based resources according to pedagogical aims rather than market logic. This framing also carries an eco-sustainable dimension that cannot be ignored. AI systems are among the most resource-intensive technologies ever deployed in educational contexts, with substantial energy, water, and infrastructural costs 183 . Introducing them into schools without accounting for these costs risks reproducing, at a larger scale, the same logic of resource exploitation that education is increasingly called upon to counter. A multi-technological ecological approach implies instead a principle of deliberate use: combining tools according to their pedagogical affordances, sharing resources across learners and generations, and treating AI as one component among many rather than as a default infrastructure: using, not abusing, the technological resources available 184 , 185 . Seen in this light, GenAI represents less a ready-made solution than a diagnostic catalyst. It exposes longstanding tensions between educational systems organised around efficiency and performance and the broader developmental aims education is meant to serve: agency, critical judgment, collaboration, and meaningful participation in shared epistemic practices. These tensions are not new: AI makes them impossible to ignore. Addressing them requires shifting the central question from how to integrate AI into existing schools to how schooling itself should be reimagined in light of what we know about cognition, learning, and the ecological conditions that sustain both. The answer, we suggest, lies not in the adoption of any single technology, but in the deliberate design of plural technological ecologies, combining embodied, social, material, and digital resources, that only together are capable of supporting the full range of human learning and development. AI is neither saviour nor threat. It is a stress test for education, exposing the limits of existing models and compelling a reconsideration of their aims, foundations, and ecological responsibilities. It is one tool among many. Above all, it is a catalyst for reimagining the technological arrangements that structure every day at school.

items.abstract_text: This study examined the relationships among generative AI-supported learning, cognitive offloading, metacognitive awareness, and students’ learning regulation among university students in Pakistan. A quantitative cross-sectional research design was employed, and data were collected from 293 university students through a self-administered online questionnaire distributed using Google Forms. The collected data were organized in Microsoft Excel and analyzed using IBM SPSS Statistics. Descriptive statistics were used to summarize demographic characteristics, Pearson correlation was applied to examine relationships between variables, and simple linear regression was conducted to assess predictive relationships. The illustrative analysis indicated a positive association between generative AI-supported learning and metacognitive awareness (β = 0.478, p = .001), with the regression model explaining 22.8% of the variance in metacognitive awareness (R² = 0.228). Cognitive offloading was positively associated with students’ learning regulation (r = 0.436, p = .001), while metacognitive awareness positively predicted learning regulation (β = 0.568, p = .001), explaining 32.3% of its variance (R² = 0.323). These findings highlight the potential relevance of generative AI use and metacognitive awareness to students’ learning regulation. The study emphasizes that AI tools should support, rather than replace, independent thinking, critical evaluation, and active learning. Educators may use these insights to design learning activities that promote reflection, self-monitoring, and responsible AI use. The study also provides a basis for future research examining these relationships across different academic disciplines and educational settings. However, the cross-sectional design limits causal interpretations and does not establish changes in learning regulation over time.

items.abstract_text: The increasing integration of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) into higher education has altered how students access information, complete academic tasks, and participate in learning activities. Alongside these opportunities, GenAI introduces technology-related demands that may be associated with students' learning engagement. This study examined the relationship between generative AI technostress and learning engagement, with academic adaptability examined as a statistical mediator and AI literacy as a moderator of this relationship. A quantitative cross-sectional research design was adopted. Using nonprobability convenience sampling, data were collected through an online self-report questionnaire administered via Wenjuanxing to undergraduate students with experience using GenAI for academic purposes at Northeast Normal University in China. A total of 529 valid responses were analyzed using structural equation modeling and bootstrap-based conditional process analysis. Generative AI technostress was negatively associated with academic adaptability and learning engagement, whereas academic adaptability was positively associated with learning engagement. A significant indirect association between generative AI technostress and learning engagement through academic adaptability was identified, while the direct association remained significant. AI literacy also moderated the negative association between generative AI technostress and academic adaptability, with a weaker negative association observed among students reporting higher AI literacy. The conditional indirect association through academic adaptability was stronger at lower levels of AI literacy. Taken together, the findings indicate that the relationship between generative AI technostress and learning engagement is associated with students' capacity to adapt to changing academic demands and varies according to their level of AI literacy.

The study protocol was formally reviewed and approved by the Academic Ethics Committee of the College of Psychology at Northeast Normal University, Ethical Review Approval Number 2025093. The questionnaire was administered in a fixed sequence for all participants. Participants first completed demographic and generative AI use questions, followed by the measures of generative AI technostress, academic adaptability, learning engagement, and AI literacy. A total of 580 questionnaires were submitted. Before the substantive analyses, all responses were screened for completeness and response quality. Questionnaires were excluded when they contained substantial missing responses, when the total completion time was shorter than 60 s, or when the response pattern indicated highly repetitive or mechanically patterned responding. Patterned responses included selecting the same response option across all or nearly all scale items and completing long consecutive blocks of items using the same response category before systematically switching to another category. A completion time of less than 60 s was considered insufficient for participants to adequately read and respond to the full questionnaire. After applying these screening criteria, 51 questionnaires were excluded: 11 were incomplete, 18 were completed in less than 60 s, and 22 showed clear patterned responding. Consequently, 529 valid questionnaires were retained, resulting in a valid response rate of 91.21%. Although no formal a priori power analysis was conducted, the final sample of 529 participants was considered adequate for the proposed CFA, SEM, and bootstrap-based conditional process analyses given the complexity of the models and the stable estimation of model parameters. The final sample included 203 female students and 326 male students. In terms of academic year, 199 participants were freshmen, 162 were sophomores, 105 were juniors, and 63 were seniors. The sample comprised 174 students from science disciplines, 185 from engineering, and 170 from humanities and liberal arts. Regarding weekly generative AI use duration, 88 participants reported 8 h or less per week, 157 reported 9 to 21 h, 170 reported 22 to 28 h, and 114 reported more than 28 h. The primary generative AI tools reported by participants included Doubao, DeepSeek, ChatGPT, and Gemini. Detailed sample characteristics are presented in Table 1 . All constructs were measured using established instruments. Participants responded to all measurement items using a five-point Likert scale ranging from 1 = strongly disagree to 5 = strongly agree. Adaptation was limited to wording necessary to make the instruments appropriate for the context of generative AI-supported learning, while the conceptual meaning and construct coverage of the original measures were retained. Before the main data collection, the adapted questionnaire underwent two expert review for content validity. The experts examined whether the adapted wording remained consistent with the constructs represented in the original instruments and whether the items were clear and appropriate for university students using generative AI in academic contexts. Particular attention was given to items in which general references to technology or technology-enhanced learning were replaced with references to generative AI-supported learning. Revisions were made in response to the expert review where wording required clarification, while changes that would alter the substantive meaning of the original items were avoided. Generative AI technostress (GT) was measured using a four-item measure adapted from the university students’ technostress scale developed by Wang et al. (2020) . The original scale was developed for technology-enhanced learning environments and conceptualized technostress as the psychological pressure arising when students perceive a mismatch between their personal capabilities and technology-related learning demands or between their learning needs and the support provided by technology. The adapted items assessed difficulties in responding to AI-related learning requirements, adjusting established learning habits, investing additional time and effort, and managing disruptions associated with generative AI-supported learning. For example, one adapted item stated, “When using generative AI to complete learning tasks, I often find its functions or operations difficult to understand.” Higher scores indicated greater perceived technostress associated with the academic use of generative AI.
