analysis.results: Prior to the structural analyses, Pearson correlations were calculated among the four principal study variables: generative AI technostress, academic adaptability, learning engagement, and AI literacy. As demonstrated in Table 2 , the bivariate correlations among these primary variables align closely with the hypothesized directional relationships. Generative AI technostress displayed a negative statistical relationship with academic adaptability and learning engagement. Academic adaptability showed a positive association with learning engagement. AI literacy maintained a positive correlation with both academic adaptability and learning engagement, while demonstrating a comparatively weak relationship with generative AI technostress. All correlation coefficients among the variables remained well within conventional parameters, with none of the pairwise correlations exceeded 0.70, suggesting no indication of severe bivariate collinearity among the principal study variables. Correlation matrix for Pearson correlations among study variables. N = 529. GT = Generative AI technostress; AA = Academic Adaptability; LE = Learning Engagement; AL = AI Literacy. ** p < 0.01, *** p < 0.001. A confirmatory factor analysis (CFA) was conducted to examine the adequacy of the four-factor measurement model comprising generative AI technostress, academic adaptability, learning engagement, and AI literacy. Generative AI technostress was represented by its four individual items, whereas academic adaptability, learning engagement, and AI literacy were represented by three, five, and four item parcels, respectively, as described in the Method section. Reliability and convergent validity analyses were further conducted. As shown in Table 3 , all constructs demonstrated satisfactory internal consistency. McDonald’s omega coefficients ranged from 0.828 to 0.906, exceeding the recommended value of 0.70. Composite reliability values ranged from 0.828 to 0.911, indicating satisfactory construct reliability. The average variance extracted (AVE) values ranged from 0.547 to 0.705, exceeding the recommended threshold of 0.50. These results support the convergent validity of the measurement model. Discriminant validity was verified through the application of the Fornell-Larcker criterion along with the assessment of the heterotrait-monotrait ratio (HTMT). As displayed within the matrix in Table 4 , the square roots of the average variance extracted values for each construct exceeded the baseline correlation coefficients found between that construct and any alternative variables, satisfying the Fornell-Larcker requirements. To be exact, the square root of the average variance extracted was 0.740 for generative AI technostress, 0.840 for academic adaptability, 0.820 for learning engagement, and 0.814 for AI literacy. Discriminant validity evaluation using Fornell-Larcker and HTMT criteria. Complementing these results, the heterotrait-monotrait ratio values generated across the variable pairings ranged safely between 0.134 and 0.582. These coefficients remain comfortably beneath the standard conservative threshold of 0.85, establishing that the four targeted constructs are empirically distinct and represent unique concepts within the broader research model. Because the study adopted a cross-sectional self-report questionnaire design, potential common method bias was examined. Harman’s single-factor test was conducted. The first unrotated factor accounted for 39.36% of the total variance, which was below the commonly used threshold of 40% ( Podsakoff et al., 2003 ). This result suggests that common method bias was unlikely to substantially influence the findings. Second, confirmatory factor analysis was conducted to compare the hypothesized four-factor model with a single-factor model. The four-factor model demonstrated excellent fit: χ2 = 147.811, df = 98, CFI = 0.990, TLI = 0.987, RMSEA = 0.031, SRMR = 0.024. In contrast, the single-factor model showed substantially poorer fit: χ2 = 2193.259, df = 104, CFI = 0.568, TLI = 0.502, RMSEA = 0.195, SRMR = 0.153. The substantial difference between the two models indicates that the measurement structure was unlikely to be explained by a single underlying factor. Taken together, these results did not indicate that a single common factor dominated the covariance among the study variables. Following confirmation of the reliability and validity of the measurement framework, structural equation modeling was executed to investigate the hypothesized pathways linking generative AI technostress, academic adaptability, and learning engagement. To isolate these core relationships, individual characteristics including gender, academic year, major type, and weekly AI use duration were introduced into the model as control variables. The structural path coefficients and matching hypothesis outcomes are consolidated in Table 5 . Structural model results of hypothesized relationships. GT = Generative AI Technostress; AA = Academic Adaptability; LE = Learning Engagement. B = unstandardized coefficient; β = standardized coefficient. As shown in Table 5 , generative AI technostress was negatively associated with academic adaptability ( β = −0.445, p < 0.001). This result indicates that students reporting higher levels of perceived AI-related technological stress tended to report lower levels of academic adaptability. Therefore, H2 was supported. Academic adaptability was positively associated with learning engagement ( β = 0.434, p < 0.001), suggesting that students with stronger adaptability tendencies tended to demonstrate higher levels of engagement in learning activities. Therefore, H3 was supported. In addition, generative AI technostress showed a negative association with learning engagement ( β = −0.325, p < 0.001), supporting H1. Taken together, these findings indicate that generative AI technostress was statistically related to both students’ adaptability experiences and their engagement levels. To examine whether the association between generative AI technostress and learning engagement was statistically indirect through academic adaptability, a bootstrap mediation analysis was conducted using 5,000 resamples. The direct, indirect, and total effect values calculated through this procedure are displayed in Table 6 . Bootstrap mediation analysis of academic adaptability. The indirect association between generative AI technostress and learning engagement remained statistically significant after including academic adaptability (Estimate = −0.135, p < 0.001). Therefore, the results were consistent with academic adaptability partially mediating this relationship rather than fully accounting for it. The indirect effect accounted for approximately 37.32% of the total association. This finding suggests that the relationship between generative AI technostress and learning engagement may be partly explained by differences in students’ academic adaptability. Thus, H4 was supported.
analysis.discussion: The findings showed that generative AI technostress was negatively associated with both learning engagement and academic adaptability. This pattern is consistent with previous research showing that technology-related stress is associated with less favorable motivational, behavioral, and psychological outcomes in educational settings ( Wang et al., 2020 ; Frazier et al., 2019 ), as well as with Saleem et al. (2024) , who found that technostress was negatively associated with the quality of online learning among university students. It also accords with recent work suggesting that difficulty managing AI-related demands may be associated with lower involvement in learning activities. However, Lallmahomed (2025) reported a more differentiated pattern among university students in Mauritius, finding that hindrance techno-stressors were negatively associated with student engagement, whereas challenge techno-stressors were positively associated with engagement. This divergence may reflect differences in the conceptualization of technostress and the technological context, suggesting that technology-related demands are not uniformly detrimental when some demands are appraised as manageable challenges rather than hindrances. In the present study, students who reported greater difficulty understanding, evaluating, or appropriately using generative AI also tended to report lower engagement and adaptability, possibly because the uncertainty and cognitive demands associated with GenAI compete with the attention and psychological resources required for sustained learning. Academic adaptability was positively associated with learning engagement and partially accounted for the association between generative AI technostress and learning engagement. This finding is consistent with previous research linking adaptability with stronger academic functioning and engagement under changing educational conditions ( Martin et al., 2013 ; Collie et al., 2017 ), and with studies emphasizing the importance of adaptability in technology-rich learning environments ( Zhang and Xu, 2025 ; Xia et al., 2025 ). The mediation result suggests that part of the association between GenAI technostress and engagement is related to students’ capacity to adjust their cognition, behavior, and emotions when learning conditions change. Academic adaptability therefore provides a plausible psychological explanation for why students reporting greater GenAI-related stress also tend to report lower engagement. Given the cross-sectional design, however, this finding should be interpreted as an indirect association rather than a causal process. AI literacy moderated the negative association between generative AI technostress and academic adaptability, with a weaker negative association among students reporting higher AI literacy. This pattern is consistent with research suggesting that stronger AI-related knowledge and competence are associated with greater ability to understand AI functions, evaluate outputs, and manage AI-supported learning activities ( Ng et al., 2021 ; Bećirović et al., 2025 ; Bewersdorff et al., 2025 ). Students with greater AI literacy may have clearer expectations about AI capabilities and limitations and may therefore experience less uncertainty when deciding how to use AI in academic work. The moderated mediation analysis further showed that the negative indirect association between generative AI technostress and learning engagement through academic adaptability was stronger at lower levels of AI literacy and weaker at higher levels. This suggests that the relationship between technostress and engagement varies according to both students’ adaptive capacity and their AI-related competence. Rather than operating independently, academic adaptability and AI literacy appear to represent complementary elements of students’ adjustment to GenAI-mediated learning. The findings provide several implications for the application of the transactional theory of stress and coping to GenAI-mediated learning. The negative associations of generative AI technostress with academic adaptability and learning engagement support the theory’s proposition that individuals’ responses to environmental demands depend on appraisal and adjustment processes rather than on the objective presence of the demand alone ( Folkman, 2013 ). More importantly, the mediation finding extends this perspective by identifying academic adaptability as a specific adjustment-related construct through which perceived AI-related demands are associated with learning engagement. The findings therefore help distinguish between the experience of technological demands and students’ capacity to adjust to those demands in AI-mediated learning environments. The results also refine the application of conservation of resources theory. AI literacy has generally been conceptualized as knowledge, practical competence, evaluation, and ethical understanding ( Long and Magerko, 2020 ; Wang et al., 2023 ). The moderation finding suggests that these competencies may also function as context-relevant personal resources because the negative association between technostress and adaptability was weaker among students with higher AI literacy. This extends COR theory to AI-mediated higher education by indicating that the protective value of a resource may depend partly on its relevance to the specific demands being encountered. Taken together, the findings provide an integrated theoretical account of the proposed model. The transactional theory of stress and coping explains the technostress–adaptability–engagement pathway, whereas conservation of resources theory helps explain why the technostress–adaptability association varies according to AI literacy. The moderated mediation result supports this combined interpretation by showing that the indirect association through adaptability differs across levels of the proposed personal resource. The findings therefore suggest that process-oriented and resource-oriented explanations can be jointly applied to students’ responses to emerging educational technologies. At the same time, the findings also indicate limits to this explanation. The direct association between technostress and learning engagement remained significant after academic adaptability was included, and the negative association between technostress and adaptability remained significant even at higher levels of AI literacy. Academic adaptability and AI literacy therefore explain only part of the observed relationships. Other psychological resources, institutional conditions, learning demands, and forms of AI experience may also be relevant, which defines an important boundary of the present theoretical model. The negative association between generative AI technostress and learning engagement suggests that university management and lecturers should consider students’ experiences of AI-related demands alongside the availability of AI tools. analysis.limitations: First, this study adopted a cross-sectional research design. Therefore, the observed relationships among generative AI technostress, academic adaptability, learning engagement, and AI literacy should not be interpreted as evidence of causal relationships. Future research may employ longitudinal designs or experimental approaches to examine how these relationships develop over time. Second, all variables were measured through self-reported questionnaires, which may introduce response bias. Although statistical procedures were used to assess common method bias, future studies could combine self-report measures with behavioral indicators such as AI usage records, learning activity data, or instructor evaluations. The measures were also administered in a fixed order rather than a randomized order, which may have introduced order effects or response fatigue. Future research could randomize measurement blocks or use counterbalanced questionnaire versions. In addition, although the adapted questionnaire underwent expert review for content validity, a separate formal pilot study was not conducted. Future studies could use an independent pilot sample to further examine item clarity and response processes before full-scale administration. Third, the sample was drawn from a single university in China. The observed relationships should therefore be interpreted within this institutional and cultural context. Future studies may examine whether similar patterns are observed across universities, countries, academic disciplines, and educational systems. Fourth, the study focused on academic adaptability as the principal explanatory mechanism and AI literacy as the moderating resource. Other psychological and contextual factors may also be relevant, including AI anxiety, self-efficacy, perceived autonomy, learning strategies, institutional guidance, and previous AI experience. Examining these factors may provide a broader account of variation in students’ responses to GenAI-mediated learning environments.

items.abstract_text: Distributed learning environments address the constraints of fixed locations and schedules in traditional education, offering diverse teaching approaches, including online, blended, and lifelong learning. Learners can make the most of fragmented learning opportunities by engaging in a range of learning activities. At the same time, generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) offers real-time interaction, personalized adaptation, and dynamic learning opportunities, potentially creating more flexible learning pathways in distributed learning environments. AI-generated feedback may also support learners' engagement in the learning process. Feedback literacy and self-regulated learning may play important roles in supporting learners' sustained engagement. This paper explores how feedback literacy and self-regulated learning may shape the relationship between generative AI feedback and learner engagement in distributed learning environments. It also proposes an integrated educational framework that combines AI-enhanced feedback, competency development, and instructional monitoring and support to promote sustained learning engagement.

items.abstract_text: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) has entered education faster than the theoretical and methodological frameworks used to evaluate it. This critical integrative review asks a more consequential question than whether GenAI ‘works’: under what pedagogical conditions can it augment learning without displacing learner agency, epistemic responsibility, and higher-order cognition? A purposive corpus of 56 distinct sources was synthesized, spanning foundational theories of experiential, sociocultural, situated, distributed, social-cognitive, cognitive-load, self-regulated, and technology-mediated learning; established technology-acceptance models; artificial-intelligence-in-education and AI-literacy frameworks; policy guidance; and empirical, systematic-review, and meta-analytic evidence published through 2026. The synthesis indicates that GenAI is most defensibly conceptualized as a fallible cognitive artifact embedded in a distributed learning system rather than as an autonomous epistemic authority. Positive effects on achievement, motivation, engagement, creativity, and higher-order thinking are increasingly supported, but they are conditional on task design, scaffolding, interaction quality, verification practices, AI literacy, and sustained human oversight. Evidence for metacognitive improvement remains weaker, while unstructured use can promote cognitive offloading, overconfidence, dependency, and integrity risks. To integrate these findings, this article proposes the Human–AI Pedagogical Agency Framework (HAPAF), composed of five interacting layers: epistemic positioning, learner agency, interaction design, verification, and governance. The framework reframes effective GenAI integration as an agency-preserving pedagogical design problem rather than a tool-adoption problem.

reading.interpretation: Generative AI should not be evaluated as though it were a conventional educational technology whose value can be inferred from frequency of use, satisfaction, or access. It changes the distribution of cognitive work. The relevant educational unit is therefore the learner-AI-task-evidence system. Across the theoretical literature and increasingly mature empirical evidence, one conclusion is consistent: GenAI can improve educational performance, engagement, motivation, creativity, and some forms of higher-order thinking, but these benefits are conditional rather than automatic. The most important condition is preservation of learner agency. Foundational theories of experiential, sociocultural, situated, distributed, and self-regulated learning converge on the idea that learners develop through activity, mediation, participation, monitoring, and reconstruction. GenAI is compatible with these traditions when it expands the range of explanations, feedback, representations, and practice available to the learner while leaving epistemic judgment and goaldirected regulation intact. It conflicts with them when it supplies finished intellectual products that learners cannot explain, verify, or transfer. Recent meta-analyses support a cautious positive assessment. GenAI interventions generally improve achievement and motivational outcomes, and evidence for higher-order thinking is increasingly favorable. However, metacognitive improvement is less certain, and recent synthesis shows that poorly structured use can promote cognitive offloading. Consequently, future research should prioritize delayed and transfer outcomes, objective measures of learning, process data describing what students delegate to AI, and designs that separate tool-assisted performance from independent competence

analysis.methods: This study adopted a critical integrative review design. The purpose was not to estimate a new pooled effect or claim exhaustive coverage of all GenAI publications; rather, it was to construct a theoretically coherent explanation of why educational effects differ across contexts and how those differences can be translated into testable design propositions. The analytical corpus comprised 56 distinct sources. Foundational sources were included when they supplied concepts necessary to interpret human learning and technology-mediated cognition: experience and inquiry (Dewey, 1938) , sociocultural mediation (Vygotsky, 1978) , situated participation (Lave & Wenger, 1991) , distributed cognition (Salomon, 1993; Hutchins, 1995) , social cognitive agency (Bandura, 1986) , cognitive load (Sweller, 1988) , self-regulated learning (Zimmerman, 2002; Zimmerman & Schunk, 2011) , multimedia learning (Mayer, 2021) , and connectivist accounts of learning in digital networks (Siemens, 2005) . Contemporary theoretical sources were added to explain technology integration and adoption (Davis, 1989; Mishra & Koehler, 2006; Venkatesh et al., 2003) , the development of AI in education (Holmes et al., 2019; Luckin et al., 2016; Ouyang & Jiao, 2021; Zawacki-Richter et al., 2019) , and AI literacy and competency (Miao & Cukurova, 2024; Miao et al., 2024; Ng et al., 2021; Tzirides et al., 2024) . The evidence layer prioritized peer-reviewed studies and reviews directly addressing GenAI or advanced conversational AI in educational settings, supplemented by international guidance on ethics and educational governance. The corpus therefore included early conceptual and case-study work (Cotton et al., 2024; Farrokhnia et al., 2024; Kasneci et al., 2023; Tlili et al., 2023) , student adoption and perception studies (Chan & Hu, 2023; Stöhr et al., 2024; Strzelecki, 2024; Tiwari et al., 2024) , empirical studies of learning processes and outcomes (Bai & Wang, 2025; Essel et al., 2024; Fan et al., 2025; Ng et al., 2024; Tossell et al., 2024; Urban et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2024; Youssef et al., 2024) , and higher-level evidence syntheses (Albadarin et al., 2024; Baig & Yadegaridehkordi, 2024; Bhullar et al., 2024; Chen & Cheung, 2025; Deng et al., 2025; Li et al., 2026; Liu et al., 2025; Lo et al., 2024; McGrath et al., 2025; Mohebi, 2024; Wu & Yu, 2024) . Global policy and governance sources included UNESCO's ethics recommendation and GenAI guidance (Miao & Holmes, 2023; UNESCO, 2022) . Analysis proceeded through constant comparison across four coding domains: (a) the locus of cognition and knowledge construction, (b) mechanisms of learner agency and regulation, (c) characteristics of human-AI interaction and instructional design, and (d) boundary conditions involving verification, integrity, ethics, and equity. Evidence was then arranged into causal propositions rather than a simple benefits-versus-risks inventory. For example, personalized feedback was coded not as intrinsically positive, but as potentially beneficial when it triggers revision, monitoring, and transfer; reduced mental effort was coded as ambiguous because it can represent either efficient scaffolding or cognitive offloading. This distinction is consistent with contemporary evidence showing that the same GenAI affordance can produce different outcomes depending on task structure and learner behavior. The review has three intentional boundaries. First, it is conceptual and integrative rather than systematic, so the 56-source corpus should be understood as theoretically purposive rather than exhaustive. Second, the unit of analysis is pedagogical interaction with GenAI, not the technical benchmarking of language models. Third, the framework does not assume that evidence obtained with one product or model version generalizes indefinitely to all future systems. GenAI capabilities evolve rapidly; consequently, the more durable object of inquiry is the structure of human-AI pedagogical relations rather than any specific interface. The second result is that reduced effort is pedagogically ambiguous. Cognitive load theory is often invoked to justify AI assistance because a system can remove routine search, formatting, syntax, or procedural burdens. That interpretation is valid when the removed load is extraneous to the learning objective (Sweller, 1988 ). Yet the same assistance can become detrimental when it removes the very cognitive operations the learner is expected to acquire. A statistics student who uses GenAI to format code may preserve conceptual work; a student who accepts an unexplained model specification and interpretation may bypass it. The design question is therefore not how much effort GenAI saves, but which effort it saves. Experimental evidence increasingly supports this distinction. Urban et al. (2024) found that ChatGPT improved the quality, originality, and elaboration of solutions to a complex creative problem and reduced perceived task difficulty and mental effort. Importantly, however, participants showed uncertainty in metacognitive calibration: perceived usefulness could inflate self-evaluation without equivalent accuracy. Essel et al. (2024) , using a pretest-posttest control design, reported changes in critical, creative, and reflective thinking when undergraduates used ChatGPT in a research-methodology course. These findings support augmentation, but they also show why performance gains cannot be equated with independent competence unless learners can later reproduce, explain, or transfer the reasoning. (2024) demonstrated that prompt engineering can improve information retrieval within a flipped-classroom context, making the quality of interaction itself an instructional variable. Ng et al. (2024) compared a generative AI-based self-regulated-learning chatbot with a rule-based chatbot and found improvements in science knowledge, behavioral engagement, and motivation. Tossell et al. (2024) , however, observed mixed student experiences in an essay assignment that required ChatGPT, illustrating that mandated AI use does not automatically make writing simpler or learning better. The pedagogical mechanism lies in the orchestration of interaction, not in compulsory access to the model. The broad reviews reinforce this conditional interpretation. Albadarin et al. (2024) found that early empirical studies were heterogeneous and methodologically immature. items.abstract_text: This study examined the relationships among generative AI-supported learning, cognitive offloading, metacognitive awareness, and students’ learning regulation among university students in Pakistan. A quantitative cross-sectional research design was employed, and data were collected from 293 university students through a self-administered online questionnaire distributed using Google Forms. The collected data were organized in Microsoft Excel and analyzed using IBM SPSS Statistics. Descriptive statistics were used to summarize demographic characteristics, Pearson correlation was applied to examine relationships between variables, and simple linear regression was conducted to assess predictive relationships. The illustrative analysis indicated a positive association between generative AI-supported learning and metacognitive awareness (β = 0.478, p = .001), with the regression model explaining 22.8% of the variance in metacognitive awareness (R² = 0.228). Cognitive offloading was positively associated with students’ learning regulation (r = 0.436, p = .001), while metacognitive awareness positively predicted learning regulation (β = 0.568, p = .001), explaining 32.3% of its variance (R² = 0.323). These findings highlight the potential relevance of generative AI use and metacognitive awareness to students’ learning regulation. The study emphasizes that AI tools should support, rather than replace, independent thinking, critical evaluation, and active learning. Educators may use these insights to design learning activities that promote reflection, self-monitoring, and responsible AI use. The study also provides a basis for future research examining these relationships across different academic disciplines and educational settings. However, the cross-sectional design limits causal interpretations and does not establish changes in learning regulation over time.

items.abstract_text: We investigated the effect of an acute partial sleep deprivation on upper limb dual-task performance. Through a within-subject design, we assessed participants' inhibitory control (Go/No-go task; GNG), sustained attention (Psychomotor vigilance test; PVT) and motor performance (finger tapping; FT) after one night of partial sleep deprivation (SD) versus one night of normal sleep (NS). After both SD and NS, participants underwent three single task (ST) conditions and two dual-task (DT) conditions in a counterbalanced order. We observed in 46 participants substantial differences between DT and ST performance, i.e., dual-task effects (DTEs), for both inhibitory control and sustained attention regardless of the sleeping conditions. Notably, more negative DTEs emerged after SD compared to NS only in GNG, but not in PVT. Overall, the present dual-task paradigm effectively elicited cognitive interference, revealing robust DTEs across cognitive tasks independent of sleep condition, and a selective sleep-deprivation effect only for inhibitory control under dual-tasking. Unveiling factors shaping dual-task performance in sleep-deprived situations provides novel insights into the implications of both sleep-disordered conditions and lifestyles entailing occasional sleep deprivation.

items.abstract_text: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is reshaping foreign language education, yet the psychological processes underlying effective learner–AI interaction remain fragmented. This theory-building systematic review synthesizes empirical evidence on metacognition, trust, and human–AI co-regulation in GenAI-supported foreign language learning. Following PRISMA 2020 procedures, web of science and Scopus were searched for studies published from 2022 to June 2026. After screening, 51 empirical studies were included. The findings show that metacognition shapes learners’ planning, monitoring, regulation, and reflection; trust influences how learners accept, verify, modify, or reject AI-generated information and feedback; and human–AI co-regulation involves the dynamic distribution of cognitive and regulatory activity between learners and GenAI within teacher-mediated instructional contexts. AI literacy and learner agency further support critical evaluation, strategic AI use, and retention of human decision-making responsibility. Based on these findings, the review develops the metacognition–trust–co-regulation (MTC) framework, which conceptualizes effective GenAI-assisted learning as an iterative process in which metacognitive regulation informs trust, trust calibrates reliance, and reliance shapes human–AI co-regulation. The framework positions GenAI as a cognitive partner whose educational value depends on critically informed, metacognitively regulated, and humanly governed use.

analysis.discussion: This systematic review examined the psychological processes through which learners engage with generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) in foreign language education. Drawing on 51 empirical studies, it moved beyond whether GenAI improves particular language skills to examine how learners understand, evaluate, regulate, and coordinate their interactions with generative systems. Metacognition, trust, and human-AI co-regulation emerged as interconnected mechanisms underlying GenAI-mediated learning, while AI literacy and learner agency functioned as enabling conditions. The findings conceptualize learning with GenAI as adaptive human-AI partnership. Metacognition supports goal setting, monitoring of AI contributions, evaluation, and subsequent regulation. Trust calibration shapes decisions about whether AI-generated information or feedback should be accepted, verified, modified, or rejected. Human-AI co-regulation captures the distribution and coordination of cognitive and regulatory work between learners and AI. These mechanisms are neither discrete nor strictly sequential; rather, they form a dynamic system in which metacognitive evaluation informs trust and reliance, reliance shapes cognitive distribution, and interaction outcomes provide new information for subsequent regulation. The educational value of GenAI therefore depends less on its capacity to generate language, provide feedback, or perform cognitive tasks than on how learners incorporate these affordances into their regulatory activity. GenAI can augment learning when learners retain responsibility for planning, evaluation, judgment, and reflection. When these functions are increasingly delegated to AI, assistance may become cognitive substitution, potentially weakening independent engagement and learner control. Productive augmentation and problematic dependence thus depend primarily on how cognitive and regulatory responsibility is organized. The Metacognition-Trust-Co-Regulation (MTC) Framework integrates these processes into a unified theoretical account. It explains how cognitive activity can be distributed between learners and AI while preserving human agency as the organizing principle of learning. AI literacy and learner agency are conceptualized not as additional MTC mechanisms but as enabling conditions that help learners understand GenAI's capabilities and limitations, calibrate reliance, and retain ownership of learning. The framework therefore provides a basis for explaining variation in psychological and learning outcomes, including autonomy, motivation, confidence, engagement, cognitive load, feedback literacy, and agency. The principal contribution of this review is to specify the psychological conditions under which GenAI becomes educationally productive, rather than characterizing it as inherently beneficial or detrimental. This perspective shifts attention from evaluating GenAI primarily as an instructional technology toward understanding how learners regulate its use while preserving the cognitive activities through which learning occurs. Future research should empirically test the MTC Framework across learner populations, language tasks, educational settings, and GenAI systems. Longitudinal, experimental, and processsensitive designs are needed to examine whether the proposed relationships among metacognition, trust, and co-regulation remain robust across contexts and over time. Research should also identify when human-AI cognitive partnerships enhance learning without displacing essential cognitive and regulatory activities. The central challenge for GenAI-enhanced foreign language education is not how much learning can be delegated to AI, but how AI can be integrated while preserving and strengthening learners' capacity to think, evaluate, regulate, and act independently.
analysis.limitations: Several limitations qualify the interpretation of the findings. The 51 studies varied substantially in participants, research designs, learning contexts, AI applications, and operationalization's of psychological constructs, which limits direct comparison across studies. Moreover, the evidence base is relatively recent and rapidly evolving; findings associated with particular GenAI systems may therefore change as technologies and patterns of use develop. The review has methodological limitations related to its singleauthor design. Screening, full-text assessment, and thematic coding were conducted by the sole author without independent reviewer or coder verification, which may have introduced selection or interpretive bias despite the use of a structured coding framework and documented screening decisions. No formal risk-of-bias appraisal was conducted, reflecting the theory-building focus and methodological heterogeneity of the included studies. The database coverage also represents a limitation. Although Web of Science and Scopus provided broad multidisciplinary coverage, PsycINFO and ERIC were not searched. Future reviews should incorporate education and psychology-specific databases to broaden coverage and reduce potential database-related selection bias. Overall, the MTC Framework should be viewed as a theory-generating account that requires further empirical validation. The evidence also relied substantially on self-reports, interviews, surveys, and relatively short-term interventions. Although these approaches provide valuable insights into learners' perceptions and experiences, they may not fully capture how metacognitive regulation, trust calibration, and cognitive redistribution unfold during actual learner-AI interaction. Future research should therefore incorporate more longitudinal and process-sensitive approaches, including interaction logs, prompt histories, revision records, think-aloud protocols, and screen-based observation. Further research should examine how learner proficiency, prior AI experience, AI literacy, metacognitive ability, task complexity, instructional design, and teacher mediation shape MTC processes. In particular, the proposed framework requires empirical testing. Longitudinal, experimental, and mixed-methods research could examine whether metacognitive engagement is associated with trust calibration, whether calibrated reliance is associated with particular forms of co-regulation, and whether these processes are subsequently related to language-learning and psychological outcomes.

items.abstract_text: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) has diffused through higher education faster than the structures meant to govern it, yet acceptance research still treats adoption as a terminal outcome rather than as an event embedded in students&#39; self-regulation. This study extends the Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology (UTAUT) by specifying metacognitive awareness (META) and self-regulated learning (SRL) as mediators between the four UTAUT determinants and behavioural intention (BI), and BI predicts self-reported use of GenAI as a cognitive partner (AU). Responses from 451 students at seven Thai Rajabhat universities were analysed with partial least squares structural equation modelling (PLS-SEM; SmartPLS 4; 10,000 bootstrap subsamples). Internal consistency was very high (above .95 for six of eight constructs), indicating partial item redundancy, and discriminant validity was supported under HTMT.90. Facilitating conditions, operationalised largely as perceived institutional guidance and support, showed the strongest associations with META (&beta; = .595) and SRL (&beta; = .514) but no significant direct association with intention (&beta; = .061, p = .430); their only significant indirect association with intention ran through META (&beta; = .186), a pattern consistent with indirect-only mediation. Social influence was the strongest direct predictor of intention (&beta; = .357), followed by META (&beta; = .312); effort expectancy and SRL did not predict intention. The model explained 62.1% to 70.9% of endogenous variance and showed out-of-sample predictive relevance. Given the cross-sectional, single-source design and full-collinearity diagnostics indicating possible common-method variance, the findings are interpreted as associations compatible with, but not establishing, the proposed mechanisms.

analysis.methods: The study employed a cross-sectional, single-administration survey design with a variance-based structural equation model. The design is appropriate for theory extension in which a well-established nomological network is augmented with new mediating constructs, and for the estimation of a complex model containing eight latent variables and forty indicators. Because all constructs were measured at a single time point from a single source, the directional paths represent theoretically specified orderings rather than empirically established causal precedence. Path coefficients and indirect effects are therefore interpreted throughout as model-implied associations, and a significant indirect effect is described as consistent with mediation rather than as evidence that the mediator is the causal mechanism (Maxwell & Cole, 2007; Spector, 2019) . The target population comprised students in higher education at Rajabhat universities in Thailand, the network of public institutions established to serve regional populations. The sample consisted of 451 students enrolled at seven of these universities: Udon Thani Rajabhat University, Rajabhat Maha Sarakham University, Sakon Nakhon Rajabhat University, Roi Et Rajabhat University, Phuket Rajabhat University, Thepsatri Rajabhat University and Surat Thani Rajabhat University. Prior experience of using GenAI tools for learning was an inclusion criterion, screened by a filter item at the start of the questionnaire; respondents indicating no experience were routed out and are not included in the 451. Sampling was purposive with voluntary participation. The realised sample substantially exceeds the minimum required for the most complex regressed construct in the model: with six predictors of behavioural intention, an anticipated effect size of f 2 = .15, α = .05 and power = .95, G*Power 3.1 (Faul et al., 2009) indicates a minimum of 146 cases, and the inverse-square-root rule for PLS-SEM (Hair et al., 2022) indicates approximately 155 cases for the smallest expected path coefficient of .20. The distribution of the sample across gender, year of study, duration and frequency of GenAI use, and preferred tool is reported in Table 1 . Two thirds of respondents were in their first or second year of study, and three quarters had been using GenAI for six months or longer, so the sample is weighted towards students who encountered these tools early in their programme rather than adopting them late. Because all data derive from a single self-report instrument, procedural and statistical remedies were applied. Procedurally, respondent anonymity was guaranteed, no right answers were implied, and predictor and criterion items were separated in the questionnaire (Podsakoff et al., 2003) . Statistically, the full collinearity assessment recommended by Kock (2015) was applied, in which the variance inflation factor of every construct is computed against all remaining constructs; values above 3.3 are taken as a warning sign of possible common method bias (Kock, 2015; Podsakoff et al., 2012) . The results, which are not unambiguous, are reported and discussed in Section 4.3 together with the inner-model collinearity diagnostics. Inner-model collinearity was assessed before the path coefficients were interpreted. In the equations for metacognitive awareness and self-regulated learning, variance inflation factors for the four exogenous predictors ranged from 2.68 (PE) to 3.79 (EE). In the behavioural intention equation, which contains six predictors, they ranged from 2.73 (PE) to 4.86 (SRL), with FC at 4.30 and META at 3.75. Every value therefore falls below the critical threshold of five above which Hair et al. (2019) regard structural estimates as compromised, but several exceed the more conservative benchmark of 3.3 proposed by Kock and Lynn (2012) and none attains the ideal of three. Estimates for the more strongly collinear predictors, and for SRL in particular, should accordingly be read as less stable than those for PE and META. The full collinearity procedure of Kock (2015) returned values between 2.76 (PE) and 4.96 (SRL), with FC at 4.33, AU at 4.21, META at 4.18, SI at 4.11, BI at 3.98 and EE at 3.89. Seven of the eight constructs therefore exceed the 3.3 criterion, and the model does not clear this test of common method bias. We report this without minimising it, and offer three considerations rather than a dismissal. First, the criterion is conservative in models with substantial construct correlations, because it cannot distinguish method-induced covariance from the theoretically expected covariance of proximal constructs; here META and SRL correlate at .841 and BI and AU at .833 for reasons the theory predicts. Second, the indicator redundancy documented in Section 4.1 inflates construct correlations independently of any shared method, so the two diagnostics are not independent of one another. Third, the pattern of results is not what uniform method inflation alone would be expected to produce: six of the fifteen structural paths are non-significant, one carries a negative sign, and the effect sizes are widely dispersed, whereas a dataset dominated by common method variance typically yields uniformly positive and significant estimates. These considerations are, however, arguments rather than tests. The present design cannot distinguish substantive covariance from covariance produced by shared measurement processes, so the magnitudes of the structural coefficients, including the intention-use path, should be treated cautiously and may be inflated by common-method variance (Podsakoff et al., 2012) . A marker-variable or unmeasured latent method construct design is recommended for replication (Podsakoff et al., 2003) .

items.abstract_text: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) has sharply reduced the cost of producing fluent explanations, syntheses, analyses, code, and recommendations, but it has not reduced the intellectual work required to establish whether those outputs deserve belief or use. This asymmetry creates a plausibility-verifiability gap: an AI-generated artifact can display the linguistic and structural markers of expertise while the evidence, provenance, and limitations needed to warrant reliance remain difficult to inspect. Existing AI literacy and evaluative-judgement frameworks specify broad competencies for critical and responsible engagement, yet students and novice users still need an actionable method for evaluating a particular AI-mediated artifact. To address this gap, this conceptual paper introduces and theoretically grounds the PEARLS framework, an artifact-level verification protocol organized around six interdependent dimensions: Process, Evidence, Access, Reproducibility, Legitimacy, and Source. The framework integrates insights from epistemic cognition, epistemic vigilance, cognitive offloading, calibrated trust, evaluative judgement, and open-science principles to treat AI output as a provisional knowledge claim whose warrant must be assembled and examined. It further advances verification-driven learning as a pedagogical mechanism through which learners develop expertise by iteratively focusing consequential claims, tracing and testing their warrant, judging uncertainty and legitimacy, acting on the results, and reframing subsequent inquiry. Five interdisciplinary cases - psychology theory, educational statistics, computer science, history, and health sciences - demonstrate how the relative emphasis of the six dimensions varies with disciplinary standards and the consequences of error. The paper concludes by deriving implications for assessment design and proposing a research agenda encompassing construct validation, intervention studies, disciplinary calibration, equity, and human-AI interface design. PEARLS is therefore offered as a theoretically informed and practically usable scaffold for preserving human epistemic responsibility as knowledge production becomes increasingly AI-mediated.

items.abstract_text: We examine educational YouTube videos through multimodal metadata, such as transcripts, titles, thumbnails, and viewer comments, to investigate how ChatGPT is framed across creator groups and how those framings relate to audience response and platform reach. Little is known about how large language models are presented to learners in informal, creator-driven public discourse. Following PRISMA, we selected 52 videos for analysis. We identified three structurally distinct discourse groups: (G1) videos that positioned ChatGPT as a conceptual scaffold for thinking, (G2) videos oriented toward retrieval practice and skill-building, and (G3) videos that framed ChatGPT as a tool for output generation. Epistemic Network Analysis revealed statistically significant group differences with large effect sizes. Multimodal metadata consistently reflected these distinctions across transcript discourse, titles, and thumbnails. Viewers of learning-oriented content described ChatGPT as a thinking partner or tutor, whereas viewers of output-oriented content raised concerns about over-reliance, surface-level learning, and cognitive offloading. G3 achieved comparable platform reach to G2, yet with substantially weaker learning-oriented framing. This may suggest that output-oriented content competes for visibility despite lower pedagogical depth. These findings reveal a structural tension in self-directed AI learning: content that prioritizes quick outputs reaches far more learners than content that promotes deep engagement. This gap raises critical questions about whose vision of AI literacy scales and what learners are actually left with.

items.abstract_text: Generative artificial intelligence is increasingly embedded in design education, yet whether its use supports or substitutes for the self-directed creative process remains unclear, particularly outside the Chinese samples that dominate prior research. This study examined whether self-regulated learning (SRL) mediates the relationship between generative AI use and creativity among Indonesian design students. Data were collected through an online questionnaire from 120 Indonesian visual communication design students and analyzed using partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM) with bootstrapped confidence intervals and four pre-specified sensitivity analyses. SRL was strongly and consistently associated with creativity (β = .674, f² = .962), and this association remained stable across all robustness checks. AI usage's relationships with SRL, with creativity directly, and with creativity indirectly through SRL were significant in the full sample but lost significance under two independent sensitivity analyses;. However, the sample was adequately powered to detect these effect sizes (post-hoc power ≥ .91); treat the point estimates as preliminary and confirm them in a larger, independent sample before treating them as established. A supplementary analysis found that frequency of AI use, unlike a richer measure of how AI was used, was unrelated to SRL or creativity. SRL is a robust correlate of creativity in AI-assisted design education, while AI use's own contribution requires replication; design pedagogy may be better served by cultivating self-regulation directly than by monitoring AI usage frequency alone. Keywords: generative AI, self-regulated learning, creativity, design education, PLS-SEM.

items.abstract_text: This chapter gives a detailed analysis of embodied AI and its transformational potential in the area of human-robot collaboration, grounded in Agentic AI and the Attention Economy paradigms. There exists a synergy of physical embodiment, real-time decision-making, and multimodal perception in Embodied AI, enabling the robots to execute operations in a state of uncertainty in the absence of humans. Autonomous, context-aware behavior in the form of the Agentic AI idea allows the machines to anticipate, perceive, and respond to the actions of humans in a manner independent of explicit supervision. Simultaneously, according to the Attention Economy, human cognitive load becomes the highest priority, allowing AI systems to harmonize their behavior with the focus and attention of humans. Under an assumed cluttered and dynamic scenario, a controlled experiment validates a modular system framework of perception, agentic decision-making, and attention model modules. Several use cases such as healthcare, Industry 4.0, education, and disaster relief are shown in demonstration, detailing how effective the system can be in maximizing collaboration, efficiency, and safeness. Societal and ethical issues ranging from explanations, privacy, and job displacement to regulating AI are listed as key drivers toward safe AI deployment. Lastly, the chapter concludes with the definition of the trends of the future in multimodal AI and universal regulations toward the enabling of sustainable, ethical adoption in real-world scenarios.

items.abstract_text: Cognitive Load Theory (CLT) has been the dominant framework for instructional design research for over three decades, built on the principle that reducing extraneous load frees working memory capacity for the germane processing that produces durable learning. This principle was developed for static instructional environments in which the learner is the sole cognitive agent. The emergence of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) tools introduces a dynamic information-processing partner whose contributions to the cognitive system are not adequately captured by CLT’s tripartite architecture. Empirical anomalies are now accumulating in the GenAI-in-education literature — most sharply the Effort–Load Paradox, in which ChatGPT improves learning outcomes without altering perceived effort or cognitive load, and without germane load functioning as the operative mediating mechanism (Ramachandran, 2026). Drawing on a quasi-experimental study (N = 184) conducted in Indian management education and a synthesis of CLT literature in technology-enhanced learning contexts, this paper proposes two theoretical extensions: (1) dependency-induced extraneous load — the novel cognitive burden generated when AI scaffolding is abruptly withdrawn, manifesting most acutely at Bloom’s application level; and (2) the efficiency pathway, through which GenAI improves outcomes by enhancing information quality rather than reducing load quantity, rendering its benefits invisible to standard rating instruments. These constructs are integrated with Vygotsky’s Zone of Proximal Development, the Expertise Reversal Effect, and the Misinterpreted Effort Hypothesis into a revised theoretical framework for CLT in GenAI-mediated environments. Implications for instructional design, AI tool architecture, and CLT measurement methodology are discussed.

reading.interpretation: The Effort-Load Paradox is a theoretically coherent empirical signal that the tripartite load model is structurally incomplete for GenAI-mediated learning environments. The two constructs proposed here -the efficiency pathway and dependency-induced extraneous load -fill specific structural gaps in the original framework without requiring its abandonment. The efficiency pathway explains how ChatGPT improves outcomes through information quality rather than load reduction; DIEL explains how AI assistance generates a withdrawalcontingent cognitive burden most acute precisely at the cognitive level where management education's core competencies reside. items.abstract_text: This study aims to examine the effects of generative AI dependency and digital multitasking habits on the quality of self-regulated learning (SRL) among university students, both individually and jointly. The study employed a quantitative approach involving 300 active students from five study programs at the Purwakarta Campus of Universitas Pendidikan Indonesia, who were selected through purposive sampling. Data were collected using four-point Likert-scale instruments that met established validity and reliability criteria. The data were analyzed using multiple linear regression, preceded by classical assumption tests for normality, linearity, multicollinearity, and heteroscedasticity. The results indicated that generative AI dependency was positively and significantly associated with SRL (B = 0.213, p = .004), as was digital multitasking (B = 0.178, p = .009). Simultaneously, both predictors were significantly associated with students’ SRL, F = 27.843, p < .001, and the regression model explained 15.8% of the variance in SRL. These findings suggest that, within the context of this study, moderate levels of generative AI use and digital multitasking did not substantially undermine students’ self-regulatory capacity. Rather than restricting generative AI use, higher education institutions should provide structured guidance on effective AI engagement, including prompt formulation strategies and reflective evaluation of AI-generated outputs, and integrate such guidance into learning task design. Such an approach may help ensure that students’ interaction with generative AI strengthens rather than substitutes for their self-regulatory capacity.

analysis.discussion: This study found that generative AI dependency and digital multitasking habits exert a positive and significant influence on the self-regulated learning (SRL) of students at Universitas Pendidikan Indonesia Purwakarta Campus, both partially and simultaneously. Statistically, this is evidenced by t-test significance values of 0.004 for X1 and 0.009 for X2, along with an F-value of 27.843 with a significance level of < 0.001 in the initial hypothesis predicting negative effects, as reported in a number of prior studies (Costanzo, 2024; Georgiou, 2025; Parry & Le Roux, 2021; Suryanto et al., 2025). Rather than undermining the analysis, this unexpected finding opens a richer conversation about how digitally native students navigate technology within learning processes. The positive influence of generative AI dependency on SRL can be understood by examining how students actually engage with these tools. Not all forms of AI use reflect a dependency that weakens self-regulatory capacity. Many students employ AI strategically as a tool for planning their study sessions, organizing course material or clarifying concepts they find difficult to grasp, This type of purposeful use supports the planning and time management and task strategies dimensions of SRL (Xu et al., 2025). In this sense, AI can function as cognitive scaffolding that facilitates, rather than replaces, students’ self-regulatory processes (Liu, 2026). (Budiani et al., 2020) found that students with higher levels of self- efficacy tend to use AI in a more autonomous and independent manner, such that dependency does not automatically undermine self-directed learning instead the two can coexist. (Lund et al., 2025) similarly found that students exercise critical awareness when using AI for academic purposes, particularly regarding plagiarism risks, with the majority viewing AI- generated paper writing as a serious form of academic misconduct. (Xia et al., 2024) further note that generative AI carries broad pedagogical potential, not simply as a technical aid but as a medium for transforming assessment and fostering self-regulated learning in higher A similar pattern emerges with digital multitasking habits. Students who are accustomed to using multiple digital platform simultaneously appear to have developed a degree of cognitive flexibility that enables them to sustain self-directed learning even in distraction-heavy environments (Nakhostin-Khayyat et al., 2024). Within this context, the reasonably adequate SRL levels observed among Universitas Pendidikan Indonesia Purwakarta Campus students likely function as a buffer that mitigates the negative effects of digital multitasking, which would explain why both variables appear to trend positively alongside one another. (Guntur & Purnomo, 2024) further found that self-regulated learning plays a critical role in the success and adaptability of learners across varied digital learning conditions, affirming that students with strong self-regulatory capacities are better prepared to deal with distractions and sustain their learning strategies even in distraction-rich digital That said, these findings warrant careful interpretation, as the dimensional-level descriptive analysis presented in Table 1b reveals a more complex and layered picture. Dimensions rooted in self-perception, intrinsic motivation (M = 3.21) and online self-efficacy (M = 3.08), yielded the highest mean scores across all SRL dimensions. In contrast, dimensions reflecting more concrete cognitive regulatory behavior were notably lower, including effort regulation (M = 2.61), metacognition (M = 2.76), and planning and time management (M = 2.87), while task strategies (M = 2.84) fell in between. This suggests that while students feel motivated and academically confident, their capacity to sustain effort, monitor their own thinking, and plan their learning concretely remains comparatively weaker. This pattern is consistent with concerns about metacognitive laziness, a condition in which students feel capable and motivated precisely because AI is supporting them, yet unknowingly reduce their own active metacognitive engagement in the process. The result is an illusion of competence that does not fully reflect genuine self-regulatory ability. Parry & Le Roux, (2021) similarly caution that the effect of digital technology on cognition are often inconsistent and highly dependent on how the technology is used, not merely how frequently. Zimmerman, (2002) framework helps illuminate this pattern more deeply. SRL is conceptualized as an interconnected three phase cycle comprising forethought, performance, and self-reflection. The high scores on intrinsic motivation and online self-efficacy suggest that students’ forethought phase is relatively strong, they enter learning situations with adequate goal orientation and self-belief. However, the weaknesses observed in metacognition and effort regulation point to gaps in the performance and self-reflection phases, where students are not yet optimally monitoring and evaluating their own learning in an active and ongoing way. This underscores the importance of external metacognitive support, including the guided use of technology, in bridging the gaps between SRL phases (Xu et al., 2025). This affirms that SRL is a multidimensional and complex construct that cannot be adequately explained by two technological variables alone. items.abstract_text: This chapter explores the integration of generative artificial intelligence (AI) in higher education through metacognitive reflection and human–AI interaction. While AI tools like ChatGPT offer educational possibilities for idea generation and drafting, they also pose risks of cognitive overreliance and passive acceptance of algorithmic outputs. Using a qualitative multiple case study at two universities, the research examines how undergraduate and graduate students use AI and perceive its role in learning. Findings reveal patterns: graduate students often use AI as a collaborative partner for higher-order design tasks while undergraduates tend to rely on it for execution-oriented tasks and structural organization. Reflective journaling is highlighted as a tool for making processes visible and fostering self-regulated learning. The chapter concludes with pedagogical implications, suggesting structured scaffolding through models like the 4R framework and process-oriented assessments to cultivate students' epistemic responsibility and critical engagement in AI-integrated environments.

items.abstract_text: This study explored the lived experiences of high school students using ChatGPT in mathematics learning through a student engagement framework and the interpretive lens of Self-Determination Theory (SDT). Using a descriptive phenomenological design, data were gathered from 58 students through eight focus group discussions and analyzed using Colaizzi's method. The findings revealed that participants described ChatGPT as shaping their engagement in multiple ways. Students valued its accessibility, immediate feedback, and step-by-step explanations, which they described as supporting their participation, conceptual understanding, and confidence in learning mathematics. Emotional engagement was reflected in students' experiences of psychological safety and perceived support, while cognitive engagement was reflected in participants' perceptions that ChatGPT supported their understanding and critical evaluation of AI-generated responses. However, participants also reported disengaging experiences, including overreliance on ChatGPT, reduced interaction with teachers and peers, challenges in using mathematical symbols, and concerns regarding inaccurate responses. These findings suggest that participants perceived ChatGPT as creating both opportunities and constraints for meaningful mathematics learning. Interpreted through SDT, participants' accounts reflected experiences that may be interpreted as supporting or frustrating psychological needs related to autonomy, competence, and relatedness. This study contributes to the growing literature on AI-assisted learning by integrating student engagement and SDT to provide a nuanced understanding of students' experiences. The findings underscore the importance of guided AI use, critical evaluation, teacher support, and collaborative learning to promote meaningful and sustainable engagement in mathematics.

items.abstract_text:
A reflective learning dashboard powered by generative artificial intelligence (AI) was developed to enhance self-regulated learning, student engagement, academic performance and learner perceptions in higher education. Grounded in learning analytics and generative feedback pedagogy, the system integrates behavioural data with AI-generated reflective dialogue to support continuous metacognitive development. Using a quasi-experimental design, 180 undergraduate students participated in a 12-week intervention comparing traditional instructor feedback with AI-generated reflective feedback. Quantitative results revealed significant improvements in self-regulated learning behaviours, time on task, login frequency and academic performance (p < .001), indicating strong effects on both cognitive and behavioural dimensions of learning. In addition, students reported high levels of perceived usefulness, trust, personalisation and positive attitudes towards AI-generated feedback, supported by qualitative insights highlighting increased motivation and learner agency. The findings demonstrate that combining generative AI with learning analytics transforms feedback into a dynamic, dialogic process that enhances reflective thinking and adaptive learning. This study contributes a scalable, human-centred and ethically grounded model for improving both learning outcomes and learner experience in digital education environments.
 
Implications for practice or policy:

University administrators should implement transparent AI dashboards ensuring ethics, privacy and accountability.
Educators can enhance reflective learning by integrating adaptive AI feedback that supports metacognitive development.
Policymakers should promote AI literacy and self-regulated learning within higher education frameworks.
Technology developers need to design user-centred and interpretable AI systems aligned with pedagogical objectives.
Higher education leaders should foster AI-supported reflection, professional development and evidence-based innovation for sustainable transformation.

items.abstract_text: AI assistance places a metacognitive demand on users, who must judge their own competence and the system's. Yet designers lack comparative evidence on which interventions to choose, where to place them, and how to tell whether they worked. We elicited 30 interventions from 11 experts and, with prior work, organized them into a design space of time (when an intervention acts), level (whose competence is judged), and source (who supplies the monitoring cue). A between-subjects experiment (N = 917; 12 planning-and-organizing problems) compared a per-task reliability card, contrasting replies, pause points, and post-problem reflection against a baseline LLM assistant. Reliability cards and contrasting replies reduced estimation error and overconfidence and increased aggregate confidence discrimination. No task-performance improvement or average within-item discrimination gain was established. We contribute a shared vocabulary, a design space, and evidence that measured monitoring and task performance are separable design targets.

items.abstract_text: The rapid proliferation of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) has expanded the potential for personalization, feedback, and immediate support within educational environments. Despite growing evidence of its ability to enhance certain learning outcomes, increased AI-driven support does not necessarily improve all cognitive and regulatory aspects; indeed, it may raise challenges regarding over-reliance and a decline in learner autonomy. This conceptual paper aims to develop a pedagogical framework to balance AI-driven adaptation with learner self-regulation in GenAI-supported educational settings. The framework was constructed based on an integrative analytical review of recent literature in the fields of GenAI in education, adaptive learning, self-regulated learning, and human-AI hybrid regulation. The framework proposes the concept of "Balanced AI–Learner Regulation," which structures the relationship across three graduated levels: AI-led regulation, co-regulation, and learner-led regulation. It also proposes the principle of "Adaptive Fading of AI Support," based on providing support according to need and then gradually reducing it as the learner’s capacity for independent self-regulation grows. The paper’s primary contribution lies in shifting the focus from maximizing GenAI usage to designing a pedagogical balance that preserves autonomy, self-regulation, and critical thinking alongside the improvement of academic performance.

items.abstract_text: Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) adaptive assessment, in which the difficulty of questions, hints and feedback adjust to a learner’s live performance, is increasingly presented as a means of supporting personalised learning and critical thinking. At the same time, it may encourage cognitive offloading and create new academic-integrity concerns. This pilot study examines student perceptions of GenAI adaptive assessment, critical thinking, cognitive offloading, academic integrity and institutional readiness. The study combines secondary literature with a primary Google Form survey of 13 higher education students collected on 14 September 2026 through convenience sampling. Responses were analysed using frequencies, descriptive statistics, one-sample Wilcoxon signed-rank tests, sign tests, rank correlations and thematic coding. Respondents agreed that interactive AI hints improve the ability to break down multi-step problems (69.2%; p = .011) and that excessive reliance on real-time AI causes cognitive offloading (61.5%; p = .005). They also considered cognitive offloading in unmonitored work frequent (61.5%; p = .010). However, respondents were undecided on whether process-based adaptive assessment reduces ghostwriting, and they were divided on the clarity of institutional guidelines. As the sample is small, non-random and self-reported, the findings are indicative rather than generalisable. The study recommends adaptive systems designed around hints rather than final answers, assessment tasks requiring verification of AI outputs, process evidence and clear institutional rules on ethical AI use.

items.abstract_text: This study investigates how generative Artificial Intelligence (AI) can scaffold self-directed learning (SDL) in secondary classrooms. Focusing on the interaction between teacher facilitation and AI affordances, it examines and refines the Content–Response–AI&peers–Fusion–reflecT (CRAFT) framework as a practitioner-informed pedagogical scaffold for operationalizing aspects of the Process dimension of the Person–Process–Context (PPC) model. The study addresses a persistent gap between SDL theory and classroom practice by examining how learner agency can be cultivated within AI-supported learning environments. Adopting a qualitative multi-case study design, the research analyzed instructional practices, lesson artifacts, and reflective accounts from six experienced educators from a secondary school in Singapore across one academic year. Data were analyzed using a theoretically informed, hybrid deductive–inductive thematic analysis, enabling cross-case examination and iterative refinement of CRAFT in relation to the PPC model. Findings indicate that while generative AI supports goal setting, idea generation, and iterative feedback, the metacognitive and reflective dimensions of SDL remain underdeveloped without deliberate teacher mediation. Teachers remain critical orchestrators of AI and peer interactions, supporting disciplinary sense-making and learner autonomy rather than positioning AI as a standalone instructional aid. Overall, this study integrates a practitioner-informed and empirically refined pedagogical scaffold with an established theoretical model, offering a theoretically grounded, context-sensitive pedagogical guide for designing learning experiences that support opportunities for student agency.

items.abstract_text: Children participate in increasingly AI-mediated environments. Drawing on children’s rights, philosophy of technology, cognitive science, and AI literacy research, this paper argues that exercising rights in these environments increasingly depends on metacognitive monitoring and control. This extends beyond narrower approaches to AI literacy focused primarily on technical knowledge and children’s safety. To that end, an alignment between rights-related concerns, metacognitive processes, and learning goals is established. This provides a preliminary conceptual basis for future research, curriculum development, and educational policy. The paper emphasises local adaptation, subject-embedded teaching, and learner diversity, including SEND. Furthermore, as AI systems and educational contexts continue to evolve rapidly, open educational resources are suggested as a particularly valuable model for collaborative refinement, localisation, and equitable access.

Drawing on children’s rights, philosophy of technology, cognitive science, and AI literacy research, this paper argues that exercising rights in these environments increasingly depends on metacognitive monitoring and control.
reading.interpretation: This paper has argued that children's AI literacy should not only be understood as technical competence or safe use, but as a rights-based educational concern. As AI systems increasingly participate in cognitive tasks previously performed by learners themselves, autonomy, critical judgement, and informed participation depend increasingly on how learners engage with these systems. Generative AI changes the educational problem by enabling complex cognitive offloading, obscuring underlying learning processes, and blurring the line between assistive tools and quasi-social interaction. Learners therefore require metacognitive regulation directed both towards their own thinking and towards AI systems, opening a new frontier for metacognitively oriented pedagogy. By bringing together children's rights, philosophy of technology, AI literacy, and metacognition, the paper explored how rights-related concerns in AI-mediated environments might be aligned with metacognitive capacities and translated into educational goals. While necessarily preliminary, this alignment offers a simple but robust conceptual basis for curriculum development, and educational intervention and future policy discussion. Because the conceptual framework is preliminary, it should be refined through empirical work, practitioner feedback, and local adaptation, with OER offering one practical model for doing so. Future research should test these alignments across ages, cultures, and educational settings; evaluate classroom interventions and OER; develop measures of metacognitive AI literacy; and examine accessibility for multilingual learners and learners with SEND.

items.abstract_text:
Abstract 
                 Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is now routine in university writing, making simple adoption studies increasingly uninformative. The more consequential question is how GenAI enters the writing process, how learners regulate that support, and when assistance begins to substitute for learner effort. This explanatory sequential mixed-methods study examined AI-mediated academic writing among 186 undergraduate EFL students across three academic levels in Benin and integrated the quantitative results with thematic frequencies from 24 English lecturers. Student data captured tool use, AI support across pre-writing, drafting, revising, and proofreading, perceived linguistic, cognitive, and affective support, self-regulated writing behaviours, perceived writing benefit, and concerns about overreliance, verification, integrity, and critical engagement. ChatGPT was the most widely used platform (86.0%), but platform multiplicity itself was unrelated to perceived writing benefit (Spearman rho = .017, p = .814). By contrast, frequency of AI use was strongly associated with perceived benefit (rho = .615, p < .001), writing confidence (rho = .695, p < .001), and self-regulated writing (rho = .869, p < .001). AI support was reported most strongly during revising and proofreading (both M = 4.16 on a five-point scale), significantly above pre-writing and drafting. A notable benefit-risk coupling also emerged: students who reported greater benefit simultaneously reported stronger concerns (rho = .522, p < .001). Lecturer themes converged with this pattern, especially on linguistic scaffolding (87.5%), revision support (91.7%), overreliance (83.3%), and authorship or academic-integrity concerns (79.2%). The findings suggest that intensity and regulation of use matter more than the number of tools adopted. They support a view of GenAI as regulated scaffolding whose educational value depends on learners' capacity to plan, monitor, evaluate, and retain ownership of academic writing. Because the study relies on self-report and coded lecturer perceptions, it does not claim objective writing gains or causal effects.
